utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Wednesday, May 20th, and I would like to say good morning to Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic, ladies and gentlemen, Defence lawyers, Mr. Stringer and his team, as well as all those helping us in the courtroom. Before we go on, I believe Mr. Karnavas has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Prior to coming into court, I distributed to the Prosecution and to members of the Bench an e-mail exchange. I did so as a result of a response that was filed by the Prosecution yesterday. Since then, Mr. Stringer has looked at the e-mail exchange, and I believe Mr. Stringer wished to address the Court on this issue, because our position -- I was going to ask for leave to file a reply on this issue as to whether we were timely in filing a motion for reconsideration. Based on this e-mail exchange, it's quite clear, because I -- immediately upon getting the Court's decision, we asked for clarification, because we wanted to make sure that we would have been in a timely fashion. As you may have noticed, we have filed a motion for reconsideration with approximately 1.300 pages of commentary which we had to work on, and we were in the process of doing that when this decision came out, and as a result, we wanted to make sure that we were timely. And I believe Mr. Stringer, upon seeing this e-mail exchange, which apparently he wasn't aware of because he's been very busy getting prepared for General Praljak, may wish to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. This relates to the motion for reconsideration filed by the Prlic Defence in respect of a number of documents. Last evening, the Prosecution filed its response to the motion for reconsideration, and we relied substantially on a recent decision of the Trial Chamber in which it imposed conditions or limitations on the filing of motions for reconsideration. And were we filed our response yesterday, I had forgotten about an e-mail exchange from the 27th of March, which I did see at the time, in which the Trial Chamber clarified that the Trial Chamber's subsequent decision, which imposed the limitations on motions for reconsideration, that that decision would not apply to the motion for reconsideration that the Prlic team was in the process of preparing at the time the decision came out. And this was from the 27th of March. I saw it at the time, and to be perfectly candid with the Trial Chamber, I forgot about this exception that had been -- or this clarification that had come from the Trial Chamber's legal officers. And so what that means is that the Trial Chamber should disregard the response that the Prosecution filed yesterday, because it's not going to really be very apt under the circumstances. My recollection is that the Prosecution's dead-line for filing the response falls later this week, I think on Friday. I could be wrong, and I'll check at the break. My proposal would be that if that is the case, if the Prosecution's dead-line for filing a response to the motion for reconsideration -- if the dead-line has not yet passed, then I would simply propose to withdraw the response that was filed yesterday and to consider whether we would file a corrected one within the time-frame that already applies. We're not going to be seeking an extension of time for that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's perfectly clear. The Chamber has taken note of your various comments on both sides as regards that matter. Madam Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to you and all my colleagues, and everybody else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday we left off discussing an excerpt from a book, the book by Sead Cupina. Do you have anything to add or may we move on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now take a look at document 3D02855, please. It is a document dated the 20th of May, 1992, and it is an order to the Command of the Mostar Brigade from the commander, Major-General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nika, could you give me the number again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The documents are in their order in the binder, from the smaller numbers upwards. Have you already seen this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What would you like to draw the Court's attention to in this document? First of all, Major-General Momcilo Perisic, that's the same person that we talked about yesterday, when we spoke about the taking over of the barracks in Grabovina, and you mentioned him as being somebody who you had contacts with or, rather, somebody who decided upon that and engaged in the landing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and, as far as I know, the other units which attacked from the left bank of the Neretva River. Well, on the right bank as well. And here -- well, the document speaks for itself. It's absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to point 2, the last paragraph -- the last point on the first page. Point 2, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a classical order, the order of a commander to his soldiers. He says he's going to prepare all the bridges for destruction. All the bridges that were built in Yugoslavia, and I don't know whether this refers to anything else, were constructed in such a way that they had within them -- they contained -- in construction terms, they had holes where you could place explosives and, by doing that, blow up the bridge. And that's something that the Yugoslav People's Army did, according to this order. And then in May and June, on the Neretva River, with remote control, it destroyed all the bridges, as we've seen a number of times. So he's just preparing -- he's just issuing an order for preparations for an attack, and he is saying what should be done, the obstacles to be set up, how the units should be prepared. He is referring to the deployment of the artillery and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Under point 4, "Engineering support," as we're between Mostar and Capljina, I'm talking about 1992, he refers to the east bank of the Neretva? Point 4.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously they thought that on our side there were a lot of soldiers, and things are always exaggerated. Most probably, he knew what manpower we had. Of course, if we had more soldiers, we would have behaved differently. But apart from preparing for an attack here, he says that the east bank should be secured and all the bridges should be prepared for destruction. And then he says that when the order is given, the bridges are to be destroyed, especially the bridge across the River Buna in a place called Buna, and that was because that bridge, if it were destroyed, would cut off communications between Mostar and Capljina. So the attack on both banks of the Neretva River in June, well, I paid attention to that. And we managed, along the Sarajevo-Konjic-Mostar road, Capljina towards the sea, we managed to take control of the bridge before they blew it up, because it was very important strategically.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on to the next document, which is 3D03050, and it's a document dated the 25th of May, 1992, signed by Momcilo Perisic, the commander, once again. It's an order for action. I assume you've already seen this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is more or less the same thing. On the 25th of May -- or, rather, on the 10th of April, 1992, the military situation in Herzegovina was not good, and you were able to see that, the way the army was organised, and especially on the 10th of April, 1992, the Croatian Defence Council or, rather, their units lost Kupres, which was a very important strategic point for an attack towards Split and Herzegovina down there. The Yugoslav People's Army, on a Kupres field, which is ideal for tanks, and tank manoeuvres were always conducted on that plateau, in that area, they managed to take Kupres, and we had many losses. There were quite a lot who were killed, wounded and captured, and the entire situation, well, it looked the way you saw, organisationally speaking. We had to work in two sections; first of all, to establish and set up the Main Staff, and this is something General Petkovic took upon himself, to join up all the groups and areas that had to be armed and that were armed, and in certain segments there were people working there, where I worked, for example, in the area of Capljina, Mostar and northwards. On the 15th of May, 1995 [as interpreted], we managed to take control of Stolac. That is to say, the Serbs, after the first refugees, especially Croats, left Stolac, a lot of Muslims stayed on, however; and the Serbs wanted to establish some sort of joint army with them, joint police force and so on, and they would tell them that they would be safe there. Of course, they didn't believe that because there'd already been killings, especially by the reservists, who were drunk and so on, and had escaped control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Muslims, the reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, on the 15th of May, the Serbs expelled from Mostar almost everyone from the east bank. The people jumped into the Neretva River. They escaped across the bridge. They shot at some of these people, and a woman was killed on the bridge, for example. And also from Stolac, after the first wave of refugees, we had another enormous wave of refugees, and we've already spoken about that. And those refugees reached the left bank of the Neretva River in the area of Sevac Polje and Pocitelj, and then they tried to move towards Capljina, advance towards Capljina along the main road. And then from Capljina, to use the old railway bridge, the narrow one, narrow railway track that was still working in one direction, it was a one-way, and the main bridge had already been destroyed from the explosives that had been planted underneath it. The Serbs didn't allow them to go through, and then, and we've already discussed this with a previous witness, I issued the order to organise urgently how these people were to be taken in. And according to the document that's already an exhibit, we managed to transfer about 15.000 people with two barges. That is to say, we used the river currents there. They didn't have a motor or anything. And this was used to transport about 15.000 people. And then we transported 3 thousand 11 small cars. As the Serbs did not advance fast enough, in those two-three, 12 four days of extraordinary effort, and I must say that every recognition must 13 be paid to the people who engaged in all this. We haven't managed to 14 transport some heavy trucks. There were some ten heavy trucks left, and 15 thousands of cars, all on these rafts. Like usually you have the boats which 16 are able to -- ferries transporting about 50 vehicles, but we used rafts to 17 do this. And the people who didn't go to Croatia, the men, they were asked -- they were told to report - and I'm referring to Muslims here - they were told to report for training. And of the group that we trained and armed, and so on, with all the logistics, Stojic and the others, we managed to arm them, train them. And of that group of people, the Bregava Brigade was later formed, which was composed exclusively of Muslims. And this brigade, the Bregava Brigade, after the liberation of Stolac in June, the beginning of June 1992, crossed over to the left bank and, together with the HVO, took up its positions facing the lines which we had reached by that time. So this liberation of Stolac, and the operation -- well, when there was the main onslaught from Capljina, was led by General Petkovic. And I would like to add also that in the drive to the operation to liberate Dubrovnik from the right side, from Metkovic, there was a Croatian Army brigade, and I think Beneta was the commander, and they led this operation. Actually, it was a joint operation, and the Croatian Army did this in order to liberate Dubrovnik, which had been under a complete siege. Well, the siege was close -- the encirclement was close up. You could even target the town using a pistol. Anyway, they went directly from Capljina to Stolac, and in the final stages, or, rather, the second half of that operation, I came in to help, as best I could.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This document is actually an assessment by the commander of the Herzegovina Corps with regard to the intentions of the HVO. Under item 2, immediately after number 1, it says that the goal is the territory of East Herzegovina in the area around Dubrovnik. You have just mentioned that that goal or objective was in the direction of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I am always going to repeat something that is abundantly clear, and that is that the Yugoslav People's Army, in order to implement their political plan, did not attack Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, each of them separately. They just wanted to carve up the territory, and they wanted to take the territory which, in their heads, they proclaimed the future state of Yugoslavia, Serbia. It is crystal clear from all the documents that the republican states, recognised states or not recognised states, is not something they considered relevant at all. For them, it was one theatre of war, and the objective was one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I've just been warned that in -- on page 7, line 6, it says that these events took place on the 15th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992 is the right year.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm just going to ask you, with regard to this document, and that again confirms what you have been telling us so far, where is the village of Slano and where is Popovo Polje? These two places are listed as the future points of attack.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slano is in Croatia, and the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia goes through Popovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add to that, after the liberation of Stolac, all Muslims returned slowly to that area, and we established or, rather, facilitated the establishment of the Muslim Brigade Nere...I mean, Bregava, that was then deployed in Stolac. What I'm saying is this: This is contrary to any desire on anybody's part to cleanse the area from the Muslims. When the Serbs attack -- attacked, Muslims left, and if any commander or anybody in the HZ-HB wanted this to be a banovina or a Croatian area, they would have not armed a Muslim brigade and allowed it to return back together with the population. They would have simply told them, You can't go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you again get into arguing. That was all argument and speculation, and, if not this, then that, so please stay with the facts. As I have interrupted, I have two small questions for you. First, you have said, and this is on page 6, line 15, with regard to this document: "On the 25th of May or, rather, on the 10th of April, the military situation was not good." Why do you speak here of the 10th of April, while we before had already a document of the 20th of May, which was also such an order, and you have not made any such observation there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I said that the situation on the 10th of April already was rather bad, and it got even worse as a result of the fact that the Serbs or the Army of Republika Srpska and the JNA had expelled the entire Muslim Croatian populations from the eastern bank of Neretva, from Konjic and from Mostar. At the time in Mostar, we had tens of thousands of refugees, as well as in Capljina and Medjugorje, and this is what I'm talking about. This is what I've been saying all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other question relates to the letterhead. There is a line which says "To" and then "Command," but not what kind of command; is there an explanation? To whom is this addressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, such orders are first prepared, and then when a date is set for the launch, an order is issued and sent to the various commands concerned for execution. So this is an order which was never sent for execution. I suppose that we received a new one. However, I did not have at my disposal the entire -- or, rather, we probably managed to capture this from somebody, but I suppose that at the moment when the moment of execution came, addressees are added, as Honourable Judge Trechsel, Honourable Judge so-and-so, and sent to these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It would then be something like a preparatory order, in German called [German spoken]. Maybe you're not conversant with that terminology. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago, Mr. Praljak, you said something that needs to be discussed in further detail. We have seen two military documents signed by General Perisic, relating to the situation in the month of May. When we read these military documents, which are quite lengthy, and I might even say that amongst all of the documents we've seen, this is probably the most detailed military order that we've seen thus far, the result is that there is a situation of conflict and that the Serbs have taken all measures in order to deal with the situation. Without going into the technical aspects of this order - we could spend a lot of time on that - I'd like to refer to something else. A few moments ago, you said that there were many Muslim refugees who went to Mostar, and then you went into the details of setting up a Muslim brigade, et cetera. Now, if the Muslims leave a particular zone, zone X, that is, where they were living, and they go and they leave without any hope of coming back, is this departure, in your opinion, the sole result of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Serbs only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If these Muslims do not go back to their region, can we say that it was due to the HVO? Does the HVO have any responsibility in their not going back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no way. The HVO liberated the area, and a free return was guaranteed to one and all, including the Bregava Brigade, which returned after we helped it to be armed and to be trained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of the evidence you're going to show us, because we haven't got everything, we've still got time left for this, have you planned to show us a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina which shows where the Muslims were, and that the Muslims left because of the Serbs, and left the territories under Serb control and perhaps even under the control of the HVO after that, areas where there were no more Muslims? Do you intend showing us such a map or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I can show you that in a very simple map, in the entire area east of the Neretva, 22 Mostar, Blagaj, the Dubrava Plateau, Buna, Stolac. I can show you the whole 23 area, because I was -- just as I said it, I issued the order. Of course, I 24 did not have the right to issue the order. Let's be clear on that. However, 25 given the communications the way they were at the time, I took upon myself 1 the role to issue the order to receive all the refugees, and we accommodated them. And all those who wanted to return, including the armed troops of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, returned to the area of Stolac, Mostar, and the village of Buna; and tomorrow I'm going to prepare a map and provide it for your perusal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll see this later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we have to clarify some localities that are mentioned in the document. A reference is made to Slano, Zavala, Dubrovnik, Peljesac and Sipan. Where are all these places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them are in the Republic of Croatia. Sipan is an island. Well, you know, all of these places that you've just mentioned are in the peninsula. Peljesac is the big peninsula that you can see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be provided with a pointer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've got it somewhere here. I've got it, I've got it. Your Honour, this is Peljesac in the Republic of Croatia [indicates]. This is Dubrovnik [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have got a map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I get something to mark?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, you can't because I don't have it. It is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number is that? What does it say on the map? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D003545. If we can have that on e-court. But in that case, could we please ask the usher to provide the general with the facilities to draw on the device. 3D0010 -- 3D03545.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We always have maps. Where are they now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We used them all. 3545, 3D03545.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the map to appear, General, the places we have just mentioned and here is the map, very well. And now you can use it to show us, and you were talking about Dubrovnik, Slano, Zavala. We were also talking about Peljesac, the peninsula of Peljesac, and also about Sipan, Slano and Popovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very small map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It can be blown up.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is Sipan [indicates]. I apologise. Sipan [indicates], Peljesac [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you please put a number 1 next to Sipan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sipan, 1; 2, Peljesac; Slano, 3; Popovo Polje is here, 4. Very simply, from Popovo Polje or from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they attacked the way we have established it already a dozen times, and it's not that they were attacking. Those areas had to be liberated. Dubrovnik was under siege. I have already demonstrated that. You can reach Dubrovnik only by boat. There was a fantastic team with some boats that managed to avoid the blockade of the JNA and managed to help the city survive all that time until it was liberated by the Croatian Army. So in order to liberate all that area, the Croatian Army had to take this route from Metkovic to Stolac in order to free the flank for -- the movement towards south. When they were liberating Stolac, they were under the command of Beneta; and from Capljina to Stolac, their operation was under the command of General Petkovic: 5, Beneta, 6, Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Then we may conclude at bullet point 2 of the order for further action, as a matter of fact, speaks about the intentions of the Croatian Army or, rather, the HVO - I apologise - and the axis of operation by the HVO, and the preparations to counter all the activities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Salakovac, Klepci, obviously the defence that they were preparing against the HVO, all you can see further up north.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, when we're talking about all these things, and with regard to the question put to you by the Honourable Judge Trechsel, what is your knowledge about that? Did you learn about all that subsequently or is your knowledge immediate, dating back to the time when the events were taking place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From -- dating back to the time when the events were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a participant. I was an active participant, and I participated in the way that I described. Regardless of that, of the fact that I was not formally in command at the time, I would go to Zagreb every now and then, and I prepared the military, both in organisation and morale terms. I was telling them that we had the strength to defend ourselves, that we will defend ourselves, and that we will launch an offensive at one point and liberate the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now let's finish the answer to the question that was connected with the document regarding the addressee. Could you please turn to page 2 in this document, and in the left lower corner there is a list of all the addressees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking to have an IC number? We'll ask for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to finish with this document and then link the document up or, rather -- yes, I would like an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked version of document 3D03545 shall be given Exhibit IC1011. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What does the IKM mean, Mostar-Mrkonjici.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post IKM, forward command post Mostar, forward command post Mrkonjici. I think I could spend hours on a document like this, so we don't have time to go into details like that during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But we had to ask -- we had to explain who the document was addressed to. But not to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the HVO. And if General Perisic signed it, then it's clear who it is addressed to, whether it goes to one brigade or another is immaterial in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, now look at 3D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to correct a mistake on the transcript. In line 16, it was General Perisic and not General Petkovic, as was recorded. General Praljak said "General Perisic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The translation was "Petkovic," however.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite certain that General Praljak said "General Perisic," but we can ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "General Perisic," General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, 3D03064 is the number of the next document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, it's a report from Zarko Keza, who was the chief of the Military Intelligence Service within the HVO, and its aim was to learn what the enemy has, what its forces are, what the enemy intentions are, where the command posts are, and all the information and intelligence relating to the enemy that had to be gathered. And somebody called -- well, at the head of the HVO was in charge of that. And in this document, apart from everything else, I think it's important to mention something that we knew, and that is that among the Serbs who remained on our side, and there were about 4.000 of those in Mostar and Capljina and so on, that among those people there were quite certainly many of those who were left there to carry on working as counter-intelligence, as provocateurs, as somebody working for KOS, K-o-s, and here he says it was the Serb intention, and that was always their intention throughout and is something they always did continuously, that is to say, the Serbs, that they use all means available to help sow the seeds of discord and disunity among the Croats and the Muslims; and that any even very minor conflict and clash, individual, to try to turn it by using propaganda into something that would serve their own ends and cause an even greater conflict, that propaganda again increase the conflicts and so on. And in that respect, they were certainly successful. Their services did that kind of work very well, and then they used their artillery to shoot at the Croats and the Muslims. And then suddenly rumours would go 'round that it was the Croats shooting at the Muslims, and vice versa, and those rumours -- there were so many rumours going 'round in that area, just rumours and rumours, and the fight against those rumours were -- was a task that each individual had over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now one more document. 3D03228 is the number, and on e-court it is 3D36-1646, and in English it is 3D36-1662, which is an article by Camil Salihovic about the 6th Fleet from the Neretva. Now, I'd just ask you to focus on one portion, that is to say, the answers of Mirsad Zuhric, who was the commander in the Dubrava area. Well, we can't say that he belonged to the BH Army because they were already within the composition of the HVO, but, anyway, I'd like to focus on that portion and especially the part where he says that they had gained great respect within the HVO. You've already spoken about the cooperation between the HVO and the Muslims and you said that they fought together, and you said how the young man, Luburic, brought in lilies for the fighters, Muslim fighters, and this article speaks about that. It says that the Muslim soldiers carried lilies and that there were no problems on the HVO side. And your experience is the same, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not my experience, but that's what I did. I worked there. I -- well, as far as those lilies are concerned, well, this newspaper, "Hercegovacki Vojnik" dates back to February 1993, so already in February 1993 the Muslims write this way about the Croats. We were very much together at that time. It was a common struggle, and he confirms what I was saying; that in Medjugorje, 250 people who received weapons from the HVO and had undergone training formed the nucleus of the future Bregava Brigade, which later crossed over -- anyway, as Judge Trechsel said, I'm not making conclusions as to what it did over there, but it was returned to the Stolac area. Well, it just left, went back to its territory. It wasn't a question of returning. And I provided them with the lilies. Somebody manufactured these lilies, and Mr. Luburic sent them on further. So there was no doubt about what people would be wearing, because it was one army, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a common struggle. And how things developed, I'll show in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And to round off this Capljina and Stolac-92 issue, look at document 3D00682 now, please. And for the record, it is a document which was -- is tendered in order to refute the testimony of Witness CU, who testified before this Court on the 15th and 16th of January, 2007. 3D682 is the number, 00682. General, it says to remind Mr. Praljak. What kind of document is this? Who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My secretary at the IPD in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: May we know her name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to this document, it says that on Saturday, the 6th of June, 1992, at 9.30, there was a meeting at the president's. I know it's difficult to remember the dates and whether you attended that meeting or not, but that is why we have another document, 3D01538. And on 3D29-1458, on that page, it follows that Mr. Slobodan Praljak, on the 4th of June, 1992, and the 6th of June, 1992, was recorded as having visited the offices of the president of the republic. And from this, we can conclude that you were not in the area of Capljina municipality on the 6th of June, 1992. And I'm going to ask you now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't think it's intentional, but I've not objected after hearing a series of leading questions, and I think counsel is starting to lead too much, and that's our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, I know that you are trying to do your best, but it would be better if Mr. Praljak reached his own conclusions, rather than you, because this was leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but we already had the document and it was rejected because we were waiting to have General Praljak come in. It's not something new.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But, yes, you tell it in your own words, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true and correct that I was asked whether I was at President Franjo Tudjman's on the 6th of June, and I couldn't say with any certainty whether I was there or not, 1992. But I know full well that the statement of (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have that redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, we need to redact line 20 on page 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm not going to mention the name. The witness who claimed that I, on the 6th of June, 1992, was at the Command in Capljina, that he saw me and heard me there, whereas I didn't see him, he was hiding behind a post or pillar, first of all, that he could have entered the Command as he said is a lie. Second, if at such small -- in such small headquarters, small room, that he could be hiding behind a pillar without being seen is a stupid lie. And, third, that he said he heard me explaining something about the Serbs shooting, and that we're going to provoke the Serbs so that they should shoot the Muslims, that is a notoriously stupid lie, because I took 15.000 Muslims across the Neretva River, I helped arm them, train them, and so on. And then subsequently through these documents, we see that I was at the presidential offices. So this man is lying very stupidly. If you're going to lie, you might as well lie intelligently, but not lie blatantly and so stupidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, as a judge I need to assess your version, that of the Prosecutor, and what the witness has said, and it is in light of all this that a reasonable trier of fact can draw his or her conclusions. We are today the 6th of June at 9.00 in the morning. That is the day you meet President Tudjman, 9.30. If the meeting lasts one hour, perhaps even two, this means that it is by then 11.00 or 12.00. And from a technical point of view, that's quite possible, but when you are a judge in a criminal proceedings, you have to work on assumptions, and it's quite possible that you said to President Tudjman, I've come to see you at your request, but my duty would mean that I should be in Capljina. Then President Tudjman may have said, No problem, you can have one of my helicopters to go back to Capljina. Is that a likelihood or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, not at all. Hypothetically, it is possible that after the meeting at 10.00, say, I got into my car, but even if you drove at a mad speed, maniacally, you would have to go 'round about, cross on a ferry, and even if you drove your car at full speed you would need a lot of time to get there. So I wasn't in Capljina on that morning. It would require at least ten hours. So the man is lying, and he's stupidly lying. And he's lying stupidly because he was saying that I was going to organise some shooting in Stolac or whatever, and 15 days prior to that, we did our utmost to transport 15.000 people. I mean, it's so stupid and so underhand that I can't even talk about it. 3.000 cars, and this document that is an exhibit already, it's something we've talked about, but it's quite beyond any logic, and it's an insult, actually. So I find it difficult to address the matter at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you didn't answer my question. You said by car it would take you ten hours. That's not my question. I asked you whether a helicopter couldn't bring you back from Zagreb to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no helicopter ever transported me a anywhere. I don't know that we had a helicopter at all at that time. I suppose we might have done. Well, we're talking about 1992. I don't know whether the Croatian Army had helicopters at all, but at that time I never rode in a helicopter, I never flew in a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you know nothing escapes me. In these two documents that we have seen earlier, signed by Mr. Perisic, it is mentioned that there are helicopters and that the Croats do have helicopters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't say they didn't have any, but I didn't know whether they did or didn't. It wasn't something I was aware of. But the fact is that I never went down there, nor did the president ever -- well, let me tell you, I didn't even tell the president that I was going down there. I didn't dare tell him that, because I went down there secretly. I had to go secretly. And even that operation, Operation Neretva, I didn't complete because he asked to see me to have a meeting with me and I didn't tell him I was actually going down there. So I didn't tell him I was going down there. I had to go incognito, clandestinely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's assume that what you are saying was what actually happened. Why would the witness have said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Politically, to politically blacken the Croats, and to make the rift between the two nations even deeper. And that's something that is being done today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, to follow up on the honourable Judge Antonetti's question, please look at 3D00684, again to remind Mr. Praljak about the 8th of June, 1992. It's another reminder. What can we conclude, based on this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you, loud and clear, at the time when the witness said I had been there, I wasn't there. I came later towards the end of the operation to liberate Stolac. In other words, I was there, but I was there later. I did assist with some things down there, but as to that I had talked about pounding the Muslims, I just refuse to discuss that. And this is the last thing I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And my last question: In 1993, when you were the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, did you ever go to Capljina and Stolac municipalities and their territories as the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on one occasion, at one point in time, which was on the 15th of August, 1993, or, rather, between the 14th and the 15th, when an attack of the BH Army was underway against the territory of Buna and when they had recorded some successes at the beginning, at the time when the convoys could not pass through to Mostar because this was going on. In that round of fighting, I went there as a commander. I participated in restoring and returning the territory that we had lost. And I remember this very well, because the 15th of August is our ladies' day, which is the ladies very much revered by the Catholics in Herzegovina. And since we're talking about that, on the 15th of August, when we managed to return the positions, the command staff in Citluk was visited by Mr. Stojic, who -- on that day, it was very hot, as it normally is around that time, and he was so exhausted. He fainted, and he almost died. His heart stopped, so I had to administer what I know about first aid. And then he was sent to hospital, I sent him to hospital to save him. That was that one time when he fainted out of exhaustion. And there was another such occasion when he fainted. He just fainted, there and then in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I believe we can move on to the following topic, which is Mostar in 1992. The honourable Judges have the binders. The binders are marked as "Mostar 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I've been thinking about what you're saying, and sometimes it takes me a few seconds to react. You've just said that Mr. Stojic came on August 15th, 1993, and it was very hot, and he became ill. Fine. But in August of 1993, was Mr. Stojic minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The head of defence of the HVO. He was the head of defence, not the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He was in charge of the Department of Defence. When he goes there, when he came, he was -- he went to control military operations or did he go for logistics purposes? What was the purpose of his visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not actually control military operations. He just came to seek information as to how things were. The military operations were led by the commander of the operations zone and the brigade commander and myself around that time, for that day and a half when I was down there, and he came when I returned to inquire about the situation. And it was not the heat that made him faint. He was exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You say he came to be informed. Well, in military parlance, each word has a precise meaning, and when you use a particular word, it has military meaning. He was to inform himself, to become informed. I'm trying to determine the position of Mr. Stojic in his defence. When you say he came to be informed, do you mean that he -- well, if you gave him information that he didn't agree with, could he have told you at that point in time in August, General Praljak, you mustn't do this, you must do that? Could he have told you that at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was not under Bruno Stojic's command. Only Mate Boban could have told me something to that effect, not Bruno Stojic. Bruno Stojic, to be honest with you, Bruno Stojic came, and of course as much as you may want, and I understand the reasons, as much as you want to structure the army, which was the case; however, communication at that moment between the two of us was 6 not as – it was not that the Defence Department head came to inquire, but out 7 of human decency I – well, the Defence Department head knew what this was all 8 about, but this was not my duty, I did not have to do it and he was not in 9 a position to tell me, you did something badly and you have to rectify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said, at line 18 on page 27, that you were under the command of Mate Boban. I'm going to ask you one more question, because I do have to clarify this. If Mr. Prlic had also come to take stock of the situation, to be informed, could he have told you, General Praljak, things mustn't be done this way, but rather that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Prlic could not have done that. Mr. Prlic could come to see me and inquire. He could have asked me, and I would have told him about the situation, as I did. However, he could not issue orders, he could not ask me to report to him, and I'm talking about the structure that was in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I have the same question. Why couldn't he give you orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Main Staff was not tied to the government. The government, through Mr. Bruno Stojic, did have 25 some competences over one part of the army. They had to ensure that they had 1 clothing, food, that the mobilisation was in place. We've already said that. However, when it comes to the operative use of the military, how it was used in combat, how it was used to attack and defend itself, that was the duty of the Main Staff, which at that time was me, or of course, lower-ranking officers along the lines of the structure as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, when you were talking about Capljina and May 1992, you mentioned the situation in Mostar as well. Would you like to describe for the Trial Chamber the situation in Mostar in 1992, when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We won't spend too much time on that, because the situation was the same everywhere. There was a state of chaos, and it was particularly awful in Mostar because the commander of the HVO forces in Mostar, the only forces that existed at the time before my arrival, was a certain Mr. Perak, and at one point, because he was a KOS man in the HVO, which means that the Serbs had staged the game in such a way as to put their own person as the commander of the HVO, and at one point, on the order of the enemy side, issued an order for the troops and the people to withdraw from Mostar. His explanation was the fact that the JNA was too strong, that they would pound the city, and Perisic did that, of course, and at the time had arrived for everybody to move out. Luckily enough, the army of that kind does not always obey orders. First you have to deserve respect and gain respect for your orders to be obeyed. So the nine HVO commanders, military commanders who were in Mostar, refused to obey his order because they smelled a rat there. They didn't understand why they should leave the town. They refused to obey the order. Mr. Perak fled after that, and he is still residing in Serbia, if he is still alive. His attempt failed, obviously. However, if you find yourself in a situation like that, after that there is a lot of mistrust against you, as a new person, and you are compared to Perak. And then something important happened, which is not documented by any document, is the psychological feeling. Who the hell is Praljak, what does he want? And people tend to trust only their neighbours, people from their street, people with whom they grew up and had lived with for 20 or 10 years. They are the only ones to trust. They will be willing to accept you, albeit very slowly, when they see that you are willing to die for them. That's what the Judges asked me yesterday. To put it simply, I had to demonstrate not that I was a general. The fact that I was a general, they were not phased with that. I first had to take the road to Mostar and expose myself to Serb bullets, and if I managed to get into Mostar alive, then I have won the right to command, because they tend to say, Oh, this one takes all the chances because he's as mad as we are. And then gradually as I started touring the front-lines, I gradually gained the right to be in command. And then you organise them, which I did, and that's how you create something -- it was the beginning of some sort of a crystallisation, and then all of a sudden people start -- good people, good lads, start rallying around you, and that's how the organisation grows, and room for rumours and lack of discipline is reduced. And this 3 gains momentum, naturally, up to a point. It all depends on the situation, on 4 your capabilities, whether you're going to survive or not, how things 5 develop. But I repeat, the fact that a general arrived, that was not instrumental in them obeying you or in listening to your orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you've just mentioned Mr. Perak, saying he was an agent from the KOS. To your knowledge, the HVO, and its various civilian and military bodies, had it been infiltrated by the KOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand what you asked me. Which two wings, Your Honour Judge Antonetti?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's a military component in the HVO as well as a civilian component. In these two components, to your knowledge, had the K-O-S, the KOS, infiltrated both these components or in all of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Save for this Perak, who was a very clear case because he was a career officer and he was chosen because he knew how to command, because most of the others did not have any military training, to be honest, Your Honours, I don't think so. I don't think that later on nobody -- because of course there was a screening process. Let me tell you this: There were some complaints about Mr. Prlic about some people because he was once secretary of the Communist -- League of Communists, and there were a lot of complaints about Blaskic when I went there because he had been the commander of a battalion in the Yugoslav People's Army in Slovenia, and then as the war broke out, he left the JNA and fled to Austria, and he did not get involved in the war in Croatia, and then he arrived in Central Bosnia across the Serb territory. And when I came up there after the fall of Jajce, there was a lot of mistrust vis-a-vis Blaskic and questions as to how come he was there, why was he not involved in the war in Croatia, why did he arrive through the Serb territory. There was a lot of mistrust that had to be overcome, and explain that all this is stupid because he is an honest man. And then every command could prove that this was not the case, because they went to the front-lines, where they could be killed. And if they survived, then they could become lads who could be trusted, because if he had been an agent, he would have not gone to places where he could be killed. However, my answer is not really conclusive. I can't say either yes or no with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you were talking about Perak, I would like to ask you this: Is this the same person that is mentioned in Mirsad Cupina's book that we discussed yesterday? He mentioned the traitor, Vladimir Perak. Is that one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you were in charge of the operations to liberate Mostar. Do you want to tell us something about them? Do you want to tell us how you organised those operations and how they took place or do you want to follow documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the thing is very simple. After the 15th of May, 1992, the situation was not good. However, I was preparing the troops for the operation to liberate Mostar. I instilled that idea in their heads. I was telling them that we were able to do that. And secondly, I was drafting some plans and because of the fact that I knew that if I had presented such plans in a meeting, as would have been case in any normal army, that somebody will talk and that Perisic or whoever was there will learn about those plans. I never, ever revealed the whole plan to anybody. I took a group, including Puljic, who was supposed to go to the north of Mostar for some talks there, some lads who were supposed to cross the Neretva in Mostar, and with Arif Pasalic, I also conducted some talks with each of them separately. I also talked to the lads who were supposed to cross the Neretva south of the Buna River. I held separate meetings with all of them, and there is nothing to add to that. Both operations were successful. We carried them out, and then first the right bank and then the left bank were liberated, both, and then the fields called Bijelo Polje north of Mostar was also liberated a bit later. The operation in Bijelo Polje was held by Miro Andric, who hailed from Bijelo Polje. He was an officer in the Croatian Army. Him and his group were volunteers in the HVO. I managed to persuade them to join the HVO. And it is important to mention that at the time, Petkovic and myself, and I also spoke with Susak about that, and we managed to persuade Jasmin Jaganjac, who is a Muslim and who was in command of a brigade or a brigade composed of reservists in Imotski on the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina, close to there; and he was in the Croatian Army, we persuaded him to join us, a volunteer, and become the commander of the defence of Mostar. This was my idea. We wanted to demonstrate to the Muslims that they have Arif Pasalic over there, but that the HVO is also under the command of a Muslim. I know that Jaganjac had a lot of relatives in Mostar. I don't know whether he, himself, was born in Mostar. And he was the commander of the city of Mostar at the time. Under his command was also Arif Pasalic, and there was no problem there at all. And the third thing that I would like to say: The first morning/night -- the third night, amidst that operation, when this operation was successfully underway, I had to leave the command post because President Tudjman inquired after me and wanted to have a meeting with me. I joined the operation without ever having informed anybody that I was going down there, and the operation had already been prepared. I had to be there. However, I had to abandon the final stages of the operation and hand over to Jasmin Jaganjac, who brought it to a successful end, and returned to Zagreb. And this is all I can say about that, save for the fact that on the 15th of May, Serbs expelled everybody from the eastern side. Bridges were destroyed. The city was in rubbles. And what needs to be mentioned here is also the fact that at the time when we crossed over to the eastern bank, or the day before, of all the people who remained there, Croats and Muslims, a total of 150 people were killed in two separate locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Sutina and Borak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sutina and Uborak, Uborak, which obviously, once we crossed over, that is one thing that had to be done, and keep on hammering to everybody that there would be no retaliation. And there was indeed no retaliation against the Serbs in Mostar. There may have been individual cases of retaliation, but not on a mass scale. There were 4.000 Serbs who remained in West Mostar, and there was no retaliation against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We can now move on and look at the documents. So the first document in the binder is 3D02543, and I'd like to draw your attention to the date of the document, which is the 13th of December, 1991. Have you found it, General, the first document in your binder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say the number was?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02543, and it is a document from Milan Torbica, who was a major-general.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I can provide you with my copy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. You said "02543 "? I've found it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The date is the 13th of December, 1991, and it's an order for engineering support. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already said all this. In 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army took control of all the positions around Mostar, Hum Hill, Orlovac, and everything else, and encircled Mostar. It was completely under siege. So I have nothing to add, that's 1991; and since then, they have been -- they were abusing the town -- that is to say, they used the reservists whom they had brought in. The map is 3D02553, a map I'd like to look at next.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Is that Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pantelic, Milojko. Milojko Pantelic. It shows the positions of the JNA around Mostar, the 10th Motorised Brigade specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On e-court, it is 3D32-0637. We have it on e-court. It's up on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can see that they penetrated deep into the left bank of the Neretva River. I don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom into that general area, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we need waste time on this. It's clear, it's quite clear. The map is there for all to see, so we can move on. Give it an IC number, and if anybody has any questions, I'm ready to answer them. But the map is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The map does not need an IC number, because no signs have been -- nothing has been done to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I know that you would like us to speed up, but I think it is important to speak about certain documents because they're going to show the ultimate result that was achieved through the orders issued by Momcilo Perisic and the other JNA commanders. So please look at document PD0191 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 5D01091. 5D, 5D01091. It should be towards the end. It's a document from the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 01 -- 0191. Let's not waste time on that. We can move on. It's on e-court. It's come up on our screens. It is a document from Momcilo Perisic, dated the 19th of April, 1992. It's an order from him. You've already said what you know about the opening of artillery fire in Mostar. What more can you tell us? Anything to add?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already seen this document in this courtroom. I showed it and explained it. Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But we have to address this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, let's show the results, how he destroyed the town. If I had a hundred hours, I would explain everything, but, please, I can't deal with Perisic any longer. Don't be angry at me. Let's leave it up to the Judges to see how the town was destroyed. And it's the break now, anyway, so we're not going to have time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. May we take the break now, Your Honours, so that we can prepare a videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We shall have a break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Following your guide-lines or, rather, request, we have prepared a video. It is 3D03130 and shows Mostar in 1992 after the military operations by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to correct the transcript. The correction was not the BH Army, but the JNA, whereas in line 12, it says "the HVO."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is the panorama of a sunny Mostar. The panorama view of bright and sunny Mostar in firm embrace will -- with the luring Neretva whose coast in the town itself were connected through five beautiful bridges will remain only in hearts and memories of the citizens and all the enthusiasts of this remarkably wonderful town. Mostar, the city of bridges, remained without its symbols in an unprecedented destruction of a mad enemy. The banks of Neretva nowadays connected only through the old bridge, one of the most beautiful and most magnificent bridges in the world. This 'petrified crescent,' as the poets used to call it, emerged in 1566 from the workshop of the famous architect, Mimar Hajrudin, and it represents a masterpiece of Turkish architecture. This world's heritage historical site on which one can see the protective blue-white UNESCO flag fluttering is endangered by enraged Serbian-Montenegrin violent soldiery. The bridge has already been hit by several artillery projectiles. It has been damaged and well shaken, whereas a radio message has also been caught in which criminal General Perisic still commanding, however from a greater distance, seeks from his sightless executers to kill the soul of Mostar, the bridge which is a part and name of symbol of this town. "There is hope, though, that this horrible crime will not take place after all. In order to protect the bridge, it has even been covered with planks, but each hope vanished regarding other bridges of Mostar, which was dying one after another, creating an illusion to enraged killers that they might create some new borders on the left Neretva bank, Lucki Bridge, or bridge of Mujo Komadina, beloved mayor of Mostar from the last years of the Austro-Hungarian reign, died first. Mujo Komadina built this bridge, located only some 100 metres down river from the Old Bridge with his own money. Shortly after that, the bridge of Marshal Tito was also killed respectively, the King's bridge, as it used to be called during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, the most frequent town bridge which connected the beautiful hotel Neretva built in a Mauro style, a hotel which died in flame, celebrating its 100 anniversary and on the other side the significantly newer hotel, the Bristol, which also burned down. And then on the 11th of June, in a fierce assault of the liberators of the troops of the HVO from Mostar, Siroki Brijeg and Citluk consisting of Croatian and Muslim combatants completely cleansed the right bank of the Mostar municipality, the enemy tore down other bridges in a panic escaped. First the Carinski Bridge, also a magnificent Austro-Hungarian establishment, which was located at the northern entrances in the town; and then the youngest bridge of Hasan Brkic at the southern exit of the town. Along with these four, a day later the enemy brought down the fifth one, the so-called Avijaticarski Bridge. In the southern Mostar suburb, which connected military airports Ortijes and Jasenica. Taking into consideration previously-destroyed railway and road bridges from Jablanica to Capljina, the River Neretva, in the part of some 80 of its long bed, has lost no less than 13 bridges. Only this information speaks enough about the terrible destruction and huge war damages, which were caused by the brutal aggressor in this part of Herzegovina in less than two months. "It is staggering to learn that the former JNA, having mined the bridges two and a half years ago, speaks about long-term preparations for a genocide scenario, which was created in the minds of paranoiacs, whereby the so-called national army already then had an active role in the realisation of the aforementioned. The bridges were brought down by remote control, and it was therefore not possible to protect or defend them. However, by the destruction of these bridges, Mostar and the Neretva Valley were not split, but on the contrary, they got even more connected, because there is no and there will be no right and left side of Neretva River."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we get the time-frame when the footage was shot, because that's not indicated in the video or on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general wants to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The introductory shots of Mostar, showing the town, they were taken from a helicopter. I don't know when that was filmed. It was before the war, whereas this footage was taken in August or September, thereabouts, 1992, because I managed to get in Zagreb, from the then mayor of the city of Zagreb, Boris Bozancic, who was an actor, he's an actor to this day, anyway, he became a mayor in the war, and he managed to procure 1.000 metres of some Kodak negative, and then I sent one of my employees from the IPD, up to Pavelic there, and Goran -- a cameraman, Goran Mecava. I managed to procure a camera and sent them to Mostar to film what they could down there; just an archive documentary. And this is the result. These are shots from that material.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to add an explanation. We have the raw material, that is to say, the raw material film, which we provided to the OTP, where all these scenes can be seen, but then there's no text and no explanation, just the raw footage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing, Your Honours. A lot more was burnt down than was destroyed. This building, for instance, is still standing. The walls are still standing, but it's been completely burnt down inside. It's the cathedral on the west bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is that the cathedral?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I think we can stop the video there. General --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for the interruption again, but it seems to me the record is not clear on this. I'm looking at the exhibit list, and there is reference to two videos with two different numbers. We have number 3D03130 in the transcript, that's the number that was given at the beginning of the first video; and if I understand correctly, the general said he does not know when that footage was shot. Now, we have a second video that I think that we've just seen, which I believe, and I wanted to confirm, is 3D03556, which, according to the exhibit list, is indicated as being various video footage of ruined Mostar in 1992, taken by Goran Pavelic and Goran Mecava. And so I wanted to just clarify, if we could, whether 3D03556, which is the Pavelic video, is the video that we've just seen, the second clip, that was taken in, I believe, the general says, September or October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain this technically, General. Yes, the original video, the raw material, is 3D03556, but in order not to just show the raw video, without any soundtrack, we played 3D3130 [as interpreted], which was on our 65 ter list with the additional audio. 13 THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I said that the footage of Mostar was taken 14 before the war from a helicopter, and that was taken probably from some 15 previous documentary, televised or whatever. Everything else, the destroyed 16 town of Mostar, the bridges and what you see here, was filmed by this crew, 17 the crew I sent down there. Now, whether there were some shots and frames that were inserted there, I was not the only one who filmed it -- there was a group of people that compiled the "Urbicide of Mostar" book, but, anyway, I provided all this material to Zagreb Television, hoping that they compile it and edit it. Other crews were there filming as well. But, anyway, it's all 1992, the end of August, beginning of September, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I apologise to Mr. Praljak, but I noticed a detail which you might have missed. At the beginning of 3D3130, this tape, it says "Izudin Sehovic," the reporter, and his voice is other portion where the destroyed bridges are shown, and that was a journalist of Television Bosnia-Herzegovina who at that time made these reportages, and that refers to the first portion where all the bridges are shown; Izudin Sehovic from BH Television, and it shows the destroyed bridges. So this is from -- footage from Television Bosnia-Herzegovina. There you have it. It says "Prepared by Izudin Sehovic," who was a journalist at TV BH in 1992 who sent out documentary reports of this kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica. All I know is I sent a crew down there and provided this 1.000 metres of negative, which is an hour and a half of filming. Of course, they did the cutting there and whatever else, and that's -- that was done by Izudin Sehovic. I didn't do the filming myself, so I don't know what went into the making of this whole footage, and I suppose other people went down to film as well. I wasn't the only person. But I wanted to be sure that this record would remain, and that's why I sent a crew to document it all. Now we can look at the footage further and see just how much was destroyed. Well, everything was destroyed. This was set on fire. This building was burnt out inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more piece of information while we're watching these images. The raw material from VHS to DVD, we gave that to the OTP, and that lasts one hour and fifteen minutes. Now, the Court asked us to show just 15 to 20 minutes of this video footage, and so we chose this one, but we have the raw material, the actual taping by Mecava and Pavelic, the original source raw material, and it shows the clap, the number, take 1, take 2, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And while we're watching these images, General, you mentioned "Urbicide." What do you know about the book entitled, "Urbicide," which is 3D00785 otherwise?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know of the book. I know how it came into being. I know they had exhibitions dealing with "Urbicide" in Split, Zagreb, and elsewhere. And what I am testifying to -- and in Paris as well. In September -- well, I can't remember the date. Anyway, I toured the left and right banks of the Neretva River, and I personally saw for myself the kind of destruction that Mostar suffered at the hands of the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska. This is the gymnasium, the secondary school, and it was burnt down from the inside, because apart from the destruction of the buildings on the outside, there was even more destruction down on the inside from the fact that buildings had been set on fire and burnt down from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the number of the book "Urbicide" is 3D00785.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can testify that everything contained in the book "Urbicide" is something that I, myself, saw and experienced when I walked around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: If we were to compare these images from the video with the pictures found in the book "Urbicide," would they be the same, would they coincide?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that these guys filmed -- this is the western part of Mostar, what you see up there is the hospital. Let me repeat. It was particularly the old part of Mostar that was destroyed, the small houses, the Mahala, the central part of town. Of course, the residential buildings are made of concrete, so a grenade just pierces them and sets them on fire. They don't fall down. They remain standing, but burnt out. I saw the mosques that were destroyed, and the two, I think, that remain standing but were greatly damaged, so I walked around and saw all that with my very own eyes. I don't think we need waste any more time looking at these images now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We can stop the video there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, a while ago when we first saw what you said was the cathedral, a modern structure, you said it was burnt inside, and then we saw pictures from inside and I did not see any traces of burning. Do you still maintain that it was burned inside, as you have said before under oath here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I didn't say the cathedral. I was indicating the previous one. The cathedral was significantly damaged, but it wasn't set on fire. You just saw the Old Bridge, and I claim and maintain that what you see around the Old Bridge, the armour, the cover, the second night we crossed across the Neretva, that 40 to 50 people from the HVO put up an armoured cover and planks over the Old Bridge, and we erected that structure in the heat of a battle, pursuant to my orders. And you have all these statements on the subject that will be presented to the Court. And the main man was the logistics person who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I want to quote to you what you are recorded of having said here. Of course, there are always the errors that we know can occur. It is on page 40, line 9: "Your Honours, a lot more was burnt down than was destroyed. This building, for instance, is still standing. The walls are still standing, but it's been completely burned down inside. It's the cathedral on the west bank." And then the question: "Q. Is that the cathedral? "A. Yes, it is." So this was not what you wanted to say? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I said, Judge Trechsel, indicating the structure with the walls, the building with the walls. And then the next image came up, and I said, That's the cathedral. So, well, this is where I was saying it. This is the building which was burnt from the inside, and it was far more burnt on the inside than was destroyed on the outside. And then next is the cathedral. Can we continue with the footage? And then I said that's the cathedral, and it turned out that I said that the cathedral had been burnt down. I didn't say that. I meant the previous building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My recollection is a bit different, but I will not insist here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can repeat the footage, and you will see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I said it very correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We don't have to go back on it. It's not really that important. It struck me, because even from the outside I saw no traces, and that's why I wondered how this -- whether this was really burnt inside. But we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
