utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no more questions with regard to this video footage and the book "Urbicide," I would like to show just one more document about Mostar. This is 3D00004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please comment upon this document for us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two things that are important with regard to these document. The first is the stamp. This is the stamp of the Independent Battalion of the Defence of Mostar. This is the same battalion which was at the origin of the 1st Mostar Brigade and then the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time on July 19, 1992, they had their own stamp which depicted what we advocated all the time, a common coat of arms of the Croatian and Muslim people's joint struggle and joint command. And the second thing is this: Here they show one of the things that permeate along the whole war. According to the list, they have 1.625 men and only 87 are in positions. On standby are 456 men or 466, but it's neither here nor there. So when you add to those figures the wounded, the sick, and those on leave, you can see that there are 600 people missing. They're not on standby, they're not on leave, they're not on positions, and so on and so forth. They reported fictitious people as being members of their units, although didn't exist, and from the very outset this was not fair on their part and this was not good for our common relations. And there were too few of their men on the positions. Eighty-seven men, that's just two bunkers, because they had to work in shifts. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And after June 1992, did you return to Mostar in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a long meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic. But before that, I have to say that the success of the HVO, with the participation of Muslims in the HVO plus the Independent Battalion, who also participated in all that, really meant a lot to Bosnia-Herzegovina. This had been a major military operation, a successful military operation, which raised the morale of all those who fought for Bosnia-Herzegovina to a very high level, because up to then we knew nothing but failures, and this applies to both the BH Army and the HVO. This is why this was significant, and that's how I became significant as somebody who never made any distinction between Muslims and Croats who wanted to have a joint army and worked towards that goal. And when Mr. Izetbegovic came to talk, and he talked to Prlic and so on and so forth, he also approached Mr. Hadziosmanovic, in order to arrange a meeting with me, and we met in a flat in Mostar, and we had a lengthy conversation which lasted for almost an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What was the topic of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of broad topics, but they all boil down to two or three elements that I found very significant. The first element was lifting the blockade of the city of Sarajevo. I said to Mr. Izetbegovic that after the operations, the BiH Army and the HVO were strong enough to be able to lift the blockade of Sarajevo from the directions of Kiseljak and Hadzici. I did not develop the plans in military terms, but that would have been my plan. I was surprised to see the lack of interest in my proposals. I am a very persistent person, and I keep on repeating things and putting questions in order to receive an answer. However, Mr. Izetbegovic evaded that. Neither then nor now do I fully understand whether this was because he was not willing to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, or maybe he didn't want the HVO to play such a role in the lifting -- in lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. My arguments were that a lot of people had already been killed in Sarajevo, and he was convinced that the international community would intervene very quickly because they would no longer be able to watch the number of dead and killed. My argument was as follows: If the international community had wanted to intervene, they would have intervened already. And if they did not intervene after the first thousand dead and then after the second thousand of dead, they would never intervene. And I was saying that the siege would continue. I don't know whether Mr. Izetbegovic was afraid that after the blockade was lifted of Sarajevo, maybe people would flee the city together with the military, but this would be in the realm of speculation. However, he did not want to listen to my proposal to launch an operation to lift the blockade in Sarajevo in a joint action between the BH Army and the HVO. Another important thing was my explanation according to which after every -- even the littlest instance that was necessary to take place between the two militaries, the rift would deepen and there would be a lot more mistrust and that this would grow at an exponential rate with time. I claimed then, and I keep on claiming now, when it happened at the outset that somebody did something harmful upon somebody else, it was still not looked from the position of ethnicity. It wasn't important whether it was a Muslim or a Croat who did that bad thing. However, as time elapsed, when a Croat harmed a Croat, that was part of the war tactic, but if by chance in a pub, a Croat harmed a Muslim, it was purported that there was a group of us against the group of them. So instead of an individual, you all of a sudden have a group, and that group with time would grow. One individual would become a big group, and this would lead to a situation that would go beyond control. I claimed then and I claim now, because this is science, this is scientific proof, that if this is not prevented on time, it will become self-inflammatory, without any additional reasons, and it will lead to an even bigger problem and an even lesser possibility to control such a situation. That's why I implored Mr. Izetbegovic and I told him that it was necessary for him to say publicly what kind of a Bosnia and Herzegovina he intended to create and what his project with this regard was. I claimed then, I keep on claiming, that Mr. Izetbegovic never put forth a public proposal of internal organization Bosnia-Herzegovina. I claimed then and I claim today that this was absolutely necessary, because every Bosniak and every Croat, and some of the Serbs as well, would have been able to understand correctly what kind of a state they were fighting for. His reply was this, Let's fight the Serbs together and win in the war, and then we will agree. My answer then and now is, Let's first agree, and then we will win in the war. And in that respect, I've just remembered, and I will quote Clausewitz maxim, which says: A war does not belong in the realm of skills and science, but rather in the realm of a social life. War is a conflict between major interests which are resolved in a bloody way, and only in that war may be distinguished from trade. Politics are the belly in which the war grows like an embryo. It delineates and forms its future shape. The third thing that we discussed at the time was for them to seek a political solution, but while they were doing that my proposal was to have a joint command between the BH Army and the HVO, because if we didn't create a joint command, people would not be able to talk, they would not know each other, and people who carry arms and they know that those arms can kill another person, become mistrustful, and that mistrust grows. When you see a person carrying arms, you have to be absolutely certain that he's your friend. Otherwise, if you see an unknown person carrying arms, you perceive him as an enemy because you don't know what his intentions are. This instills fears, and fear results in crazy reactions. Again, I did not receive any answer. The answer was very evasive, it was, Yes, no, we'll do our best, we'll try. Although in that respect, I believe that Mr. Izetbegovic was much more inclined to a joint command. He did have good intentions with this regard. Subsequently, when I was in Central Bosnia, I learned that Sefer Halilovic and the people who surrounded him did not want that. They would not have accepted that in a million years. And he did not have the power against Sefer Halilovic and other players, he didn't have the power to resist them. And I'm going to show this in the books that these people wrote about that, and these books have to be admitted into evidence. You have to read the parts there in order to understand why our efforts failed for the army to function as well as it could while political solutions were being sought, and this would have prevented a conflict. A conflict is something that happens very easily in an army. Somebody opens fire, the other responds, and then there is all-out shooting. Everybody claims that the other person started first. The commander obviously has to react without being able to verify every instance of shooting, and it's a tug-of-war. It takes two days for the situation to calm down. The third day is calm. The fourth day, it starts all over again. And this is all perpetuated if a joint command is not set up. This stamp on the document should have been the basis of something that already existed on the ground, and in that respect I and Jasmin Jaganjac, and Petkovic, and so on and so forth -- you've seen hundreds of cease-fires and attempts. I claim and I will prove that Sefer Halilovic, Muslimovic and people from the 3rd Corps and the Mujahedin, prevented any attempts to create a joint command. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's talk about Bura.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I was going to ask you. As regards Operation Bura, what is it that you can tell us? 3D03159 is the map, and the name of the operation is B-u-r a, Bura.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While this is being produced, I can say that the conversation that I had was very pleasant. We talked like two gentlemen. I gave him a gift of a military vest. He was in a military uniform. It was cold. He was getting ready to go back to Sarajevo, and I told him, Mr. President of the Presidency will be cold. Why don't you take this vest as a gift. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for the interruption. Can we just get a clarification on the time-frame? The general's been talking about a meeting he had with Mr. Izetbegovic. He indicated at the beginning that this occurred sometime after he returned to Mostar in June of 1992, and I had the impression that the meeting had occurred around that time. But now he's just made a statement indicating that the weather was cold, and so perhaps he could just tell us exactly when that meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how this is being interpreted, but I'm very precise in everything I'm saying. I'm saying it will be cold in Sarajevo. Mr. Izetbegovic was getting ready to go to Sarajevo, and at that time it was cold in Sarajevo, not in Herzegovina. And the exact date is the date when he spoke with Prlic and the others. The date has been repeated here. You can find it in all the documents. I can't remember the date exactly. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: October 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there you go, October 1992. We have a map of Operation Bura. I don't know whether Mr. Petkovic will testify. He knows a lot more about Bura because he was the one who prepared it and conducted it. I participated in Bura as an aid on the ground. Operation Bura was carried out on the 8th of October or thereabouts in 1992 - it's neither here nor there, one day before or later doesn't make such a difference - in order to repel the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska even further afield. And the operation was only partially successful. However, it was successful in that it inflicted a lot of losses on the enemy, and also the strength and power of the HVO was demonstrated to them. Some muscle was flexed to show them that they could not play games like they did at the beginning of the war. And some parts of the BiH Army and all the Muslims in the ranks of the HVO participated in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think we can round off with Mostar in 1992, or rather we finished with that part, and we can move on to 1992 in Prozor. And for us to do that, would you take up something that the Judges have been given; that is to say, two files entitled "General Praljak calms the situation down" or "quells the situation." These are the documents. They look like this [indicates]. They're not in a binder, but they're a set joined together on their own. General, when did you arrive in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict in Prozor broke out -- was it the 23rd of October; is that right? Yes, the 23rd of October, 1993. I described exactly --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, 1992. President Franjo Tudjman learnt about the conflict in Prozor. He called me. I don't know the two dates, Uskoplje and the other one when Izetbegovic was there, but it's more likely that Izetbegovic was there on the 15th of January. And he requested that I go there to help calm the situation down. And he said that a war with the Muslims must be avoided at all costs. I didn't go in a helicopter, Judge Antonetti, no, I didn't. I got into my car and drove down there and reported to Petkovic, of course, or Stojic, and Arif Pasalic. And then Arif Pasalic and I -- well, the corps hadn't been set up yet. It was still the 1st Mostar Brigade, and he was the commander. Anyway, we went together towards Prozor on the main road, and that's when he gave me a BH Army ID. We reached Jablanica, and in Jablanica some Muslims who had left Prozor were already pouring in. We tried to take the road towards Prozor. However, there was shooting from unknown directions along that road. And as we weren't able to set up any communication lines, we weren't able to come into contact with any of the parties, so he asked that we return to Jablanica. And in Jablanica, we held a meeting together with some people who had escaped from Prozor. They were Muslims. And this was in the hall of the hydroelectric power-station of Jablanica. They told us their story. They complained and said that many of their cars had been confiscated. I talked to them. I said that I would do my best to go up there, break through up there, and that we'd do our best to have them returned home. I did not, of course, promise that their cars would be returned because people who steal cars, it's impossible to catch them, to catch those people. And one should always be realistic, so I said to them at the time that we didn't have the means, the military police or anybody else, we didn't have the means to catch those scoundrels, but we would certainly find some of them and some of the cars. And then I said that the HZ-HB would most probably find the money to pay them out in the form of damages, and I think that this was done to a certain extent by Dr. Prlic. We returned, and then I used the roundabout road through -- across Vran, Mount Vran, and I arrived in Prozor that way, and the situation was completely chaotic. There was fighting going on. Shop windows had been broken. There was glass and shards on the road. And there were some groups over there who were not HOS, not the H-o-s. They were quite defined groups. I came into contact with Siljeg and Franjic and the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to ask you a question and interrupt this as long as we still see it. It relates to page 55. On line 5, you tell us that people from Prozor complained that their cars had been confiscated, and then you speak about your response, and there you speak of cars being stolen. Now, maybe there is a problem in translation, but confiscation is one thing and theft may be a polemic expression after cars have been unlawfully confiscated, but basically between confiscation and theft, there is a clear difference. Could you explain what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was quite certainly not confiscation. They weren't confiscated. These individuals, these groups outside the HVO, the HOS, and these undefined groups, they either took somebody's car by expelling them out of the car; or, B, they broke into a car that was on the road and drove it off because the owners had left the area. So I do understand terminology, but when I say -- well, they were left car-less, without a car. I didn't investigate into what ways these were seized. There was certainly vehicles that were seized and those that were stolen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Look at 3D00424 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to make sure that I understand your narrative correctly, and complete what you have told us, these people came and told you, Our cars have been confiscated, and you translated the term "confiscated" into "stolen" because you did not believe them, that anything like a confiscation had taken place? Is that how we have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. General Praljak is receiving the wrong interpretation. When you say "confiscated," the correct translation of that is "konfiskovana" whereas the B/C/S was wrong, and I wanted to explain what Judge Trechsel meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's one problem, one part of the problem. The other problem was there were a group of people there, 50 or 60, who were shouting because they had been mistreated. Now, the terms and expressions they used, Judge Trechsel, the language they used, now, in all that chaos, well, I understand that you want to hear the exact words they used, but it was all chaotic. I don't know. They remained without their cars. They were left without their cars. What they actually said, what words they used, well, I don't know. I know that when I arrived in Rama, I saw a group who had taken a car away from someone, and some witness spoke about that. I cocked my pistol, they cocked theirs, and it was all I could do not to shoot and have the car returned to the rightful owner. Now, you're going to deal with all these legal matters. I'm just telling you about the facts, and you’ll do the legal stuff. So, in that conflict, who stole the car and who seized the car, I don't know...and I wouldn't like to go into all that. I just told them that we would search for the vehicles, that it was certain that we wouldn't be able to find all the vehicles, and that I would do my best, to the best of my ability, to ensure that they were paid out damages. That's the general gist of my conversation with them, and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Paradoxically, by telling us it was not so clear, what you said, you have clarified the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what I said was, We'll calm the situation down and you'll be able to go home. But, you know, at meetings of that kind, well, it's not an academic discussion. Let me just say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a question in order to clarify what's been said. You said that this event in Prozor took place on October 23rd. As far as you know, before October 23rd, had there been, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, other places where there had been conflicts between Muslims and Croats that maybe weren't as serious as in Prozor, but where there had been tensions between the two groups which became very serious and then calmed down? Were there other signs of prior tension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. I was informed through various channels about the tensions in Prozor, which started significantly earlier, and the tensions in Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf, which also began much earlier, and about the tension in Novi Travnik, which broke out over some petrol pump or whatever. So it's on the basis of those facts that I talked to Mr. Izetbegovic in the way that I did. I don't have time to bring in an expert from social psychology here so that I could explain how difficult it is to patch up a lack of confidence that suddenly occurs, a rift in confidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again, but on page 58, the general was wrongly interpreted. On line 25, the general said that he would bring in an expert. In the transcript, it says he doesn't have time to bring in an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had understood, because the French interpretation is better, and there's never a problem with the French interpretation. General Praljak, the reason I've asked this question is that there was something behind my mind here. Prozor, in the eyes of the OTP, was part of the joint criminal enterprise, and therefore the point that needs to be decided by the trier of fact is: Was this a typical example of this joint enterprise or was it something that occurred that day, where the persons responsible were local and not the leaders of the HVO and, even less, people in Zagreb? That is what we must determine, and that is why I have asked you whether there had been events elsewhere, and you've said, yes, there had been a few, and that is why you discussed with Mr. Izetbegovic. So if I've understood correctly, you have confirmed that before Prozor, there had been problems in other localities - maybe not as serious - but nevertheless there had been tensions between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There had been tensions between Croats, there was tension between groups of Croats themselves. The people down there killed eight Croats in Herzegovina, HOS with Kraljevic. In Ljubuski, they -- the Croats killed more people amongst themselves than Muslims who were killed. So the army, an army of that type, especially when it's not in the barracks and not undergoing exercises, and when we don't know the aims, it's impossible to prevent. The very fact that there are weapons increases human aggression two and a half times, if you just put someone in a room where there's an experiment going on, and that's why I'm going to discuss this with a social psychologist and explain that the situation was inflammatory as of itself, of its own accord. And, Your Honours, in Prozor, along with the support of the entire leadership of the HZ-HB and HVO, I pissed blood in my efforts to try and deal with the situation. Now, I'd been asked from Zagreb. I had Petkovic's support. Well, not Petkovic. He issued orders. I came to Prozor and I talked to the Muslims, but there were some groups over there, and quite simply you didn't know who they belonged to. There were a lot of them. They were armed, and I had to run after them in Rama with a pistol. And just at one point, when I saw that it was -- it couldn't be dealt with only at the level of the army, just one meeting -- not just one meeting, I had dozens of meetings, but at one meeting I invited 150 people, the most important people from all the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can stop there. I would like to leave it up to your counsel to ask the questions now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just intervene. On the transcript, I understood General Praljak differently to what was recorded on the page, lines 12 and 13. What it says here is: "I had Petkovic's support. Well, not Petkovic. He issued orders." That's how it reads. General Praljak, would you explain to us in what sense you had Petkovic's support, what you said with respect to orders because from this, it would follow that you didn't have Petkovic's support.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was more than support. He was the commander. He simply wrote down all the orders upon which the army was to act. I helped him. I assisted him. It was vice versa, the other way around. I was a worker in the field, somebody who shouts over there, tries to settle things that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have a problem with the record again. So what you just now said, would you say it slowly enough so that all the words uttered can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how things stand: It's not Petkovic who was support to me. I was support to Petkovic and the rest of the HZ-HB leadership. I was what is called a worker in the field, out in the field, on the ground, implementing policy, which means I entreated people. I held meetings. I shouted at people. I threatened people. I shouted at the top of my voice. I would get out my pistol, things like that. So in that respect, I was a good worker in the field, because I tried to manage and harness chaos. It's not something that can be resolved structurally. It was chaotic, and because of what I used to do previously, as being a producer and director, I knew how to deal with chaos better. It was part of my profession. So they -- I was a worker in the field, on the ground. I had to pull out my pistol every so often, grab people. At meetings, which I explained everything to them, at one point in front of 150 people I took off my jacket and said, If anybody wants to have a fight with me, he can step outside and I'll fight them, if somebody wants to go to war with me. So that's what the situation looked like. That's what the atmosphere was like. And then I claimed that staying down there in the field in that territory, this is true for Jajce and the rest, I remained there until the conflict in Rama, Gornji Vakuf, and the entire area, Konjic, Prozor and so on; and I managed to hold the situation under control as much as that was possible, but without a political solution, A, and, B, without a military joint command, and, C, with all the elements we had whereby many in the BH Army wanted to have a conflict with us, you can keep the situation under control for just so long and then it will erupt again. And unfortunately nobody had absolute power in that respect. You can do your utmost and work yourself to the bone, but unless you have the right foundations, your house will topple ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, in response to Antonetti's -- Judge Antonetti's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question, Mr. Praljak, as regards the event that took place in Rama. I see that you were very active in the field, according to what you've just told us. In front of a group of people who had confiscated a vehicle, you took out your gun, and apparently you were the -- they did too, and you were the stronger of the two. Yesterday, you told a story whereby you put your gun into someone's mouth, a person who was reticent, and that you were successful. Now, the question I would like to put to you is as follows: Over and beyond your individual effort, what about your superiors; couldn't they have given more men to help you, armed men, to be able to deal with these situations? In other words, was there military police or was there any kind of military justice to be able to deal with these special situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain this. Well, with the car, there was that one isolated case in Rama. I managed to seize the car from the three men that were trying to take it. You did have the military police, but - you know what? – the conflict had just stopped, and certain positions were still being held when I arrived. In other words, someone has to be there as a litmus test for -- if two groups had fought and there were three or four fatalities on both sides or whatever, there is mistrust, and it's impossible at that time to reconcile parts of the army, the HVO. The Muslims were wary and you needed somebody to come in, and that was me, and it's impossible to join the armies straight away. What I tried to do was to join up the civilians first. I asked that 150 people be brought from the villages, prominent villagers, people who were prominent in their villages and trusted and respected in their villages. So you would have to -- it's a heated atmosphere and you have to instill reason into the people's minds, and it's very difficult to establish a dialogue, to begin with. From this document, you can see that a military police did exist, because many of the cars were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What do you mean is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3D00424, and that's ten days after my arrival. Here we have an order that I signed. And it was also signed, of course, by Valentin Coric, although I don't think this is his signature. It's the order to return the vehicles which had been -- which were located at the stations of the 2nd Military Police Battalion. I think that was in Livno. So they had been collected, and the ones that they managed to seize from those types over there, that they be returned. So this required 10 or 12 days of diligent work. I don't think that all the vehicles were uncovered, but here you have the order whereby they should be returned to their owners. And by this time, the situation had already calmed down and most of the people who left their homes came back to Rama. The town was cleaned up and set to right and so on. I did have assistance. Well, Petkovic wrote an order, Siljeg wrote orders, Franjic wrote orders, and the situation did calm down from one hour to the next, from one day to the next. And after there's been shooting, it's a slow process, especially so as there were groups still afoot. And you can see from a document -- well, from the documents that I looked through and that are in this file, the BH Army was preparing an attack on Rama and Prozor, and, well, there weren't many of them. Well, the problem burgeoned from one month to the next in Rama. First of all, it was a problem of weapons, then the school, then the language, then the fact that they weren't going up to the front-lines, and this grows and grows, and then they had a meeting where all these questions were to be resolved. Someone from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BH Army, killed one or two HVO members, and then everything erupted. 10 So you know, Judge Mindua, it doesn’t start just like that, there's always a 11 preparation of several days, months...Preparing for war always takes several 12 years. There's something that is cooking inside, and then it erupts, and 13 then people say, That's when the war began. But all these things and wars 14 always begin much earlier on and grow little by little, and the greater the 15 conflict, the longer it is in preparation, whether preparations for World War 16 II, or the aggression in Yugoslavia, or the conflict in Rama. It grows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let's continue going through the document about the meeting that took part with 150 people. Please go to 3D00291 and tell the Trial Chamber about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm. Well, here the Security Information Service, the SIS of the Defence Department, explains this. This was on the 1st of December. A meeting was held of the operation zone, and after that there was a meeting with the extremists from among those who had staged the conflict and hailed from the territories of other municipalities. I had collected information, and based on that information I asked, requested, demanded, shouted out to everybody to come and talk to me. And then Mr. Salih Ruvic, whom I remember very well, whom I know very well -- I found there's some people who had been arrested and imprisoned. Of course, one did not care whether this was done with a good cause or not. I didn't care one way or the other. I let them go home. Somebody wrote that they participated or not. At that moment, well, here you go Your Honour Judge Trechsel, this might interest you, I simply used forceful order issuing to let these people go, and then somebody beat Mr. Salih Ruvic up on his way out. It was in the evening. I talked to him. We agreed that he would go home, that he would gather people, and that he would come back for a joint meeting. And then when I was supposed to -- when they came to the meeting, at first Ruvic wasn't there, and then after he turned up, he was black and blue after having been beaten. Now, as to who beat him up, not in a million years can you learn that, but there was a lot of outrage. I cancelled that meeting and called another meeting after that, and at that meeting, now what did I say, what was I talking about? I talked about all sorts of things. At the end, I threatened everybody that they will have to face me. I know that I ended the meeting by removing my coat and said, If any of you fools and idiots want to fight, I'll be outside, and whoever can muster the courage to fight me, please step out. This was done in order to bring things down from very high political and military spheres to the level where things were actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So this is the meeting in the motel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: With the elderly and respectable people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I called elderly and respectable people. I let everybody go from prison. I managed to patch things up very well and put things in order. However, science will show that the next long conflict -- for a next conflict to happen, it takes a lot less than for the previous one. This is part of social psychology. If people had found themselves embroiled in something, in a situation like that, the second time 'round it takes a lot less for a conflict to break out than the first time, and this is how the things spiral out of proportion. And then I would add to that, rumours about Travnik: this is happening in Travnik, or, the other thing is happening in Vakuf, Muslims saying that we are strangling them, Croats saying that they have attacked us, those rumours were killing us, killing the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Up to Prozor, were there any armed conflicts between the HVO and the BH Army or rather the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as -- there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There were just tensions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you, since you were talking about this -- I apologise. I apologise. The question was whether these were only tensions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Likewise, it hasn't been recorded that you answered my question, and my question was: Before Prozor, were there any armed conflicts between the Territorial Defence and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Could you please look at 3D00418. You may have to use the e-court.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well, then. What can you tell us about the events described in the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was sent by the TG Konjic to Mr. Sefer Halilovic. This was written by Muslim commanders, and they wrote about their view of the situation in Prozor and how things had transpired, according to them. The document is a lengthy one, but I can, for example, say those things which are true and correct. This was my fifth departure up there with various peoples, fifth or sixth maybe. I arrived there with Mr. Bozo Rajic and the local commanders and three unknown members of the HVO, as they say. I really don't remember, myself, whom I took up there, whom I took there to talk to other people, and demanded them to talk to them. However, this report was issued on the 4th of November, but I believe that it applies to the situation that transpired a few days earlier, the 1st or the 2nd day. It says here that the HOS, and it's obvious that they were grilling lamb on a spit and that they were kicking a lily flag in the mud, which is true, they did it, and they said that I did not have the authority and they did not listen to me, and this is also true. There were a lot of them under arms, and all of my attempts -- I managed to deal with them later on, but at that very moment those drunken youth with that lamb, I could not deal with them, I couldn't do anything. And it is also true that I was visibly up pleasant. And then I started issuing orders and giving commands, and so on and so forth. And what else is there? It says here under 3 that on several occasions the general pointed out that the HVO held only Izetbegovic in any esteem, and that's true. I was telling them that their commanders, Hanefija Prlic [as interpreted] in Vakuf and some commanders simply were working against the HVO, and I saw this with my own two eyes. And it was obvious that Sefer Halilovic and the team around him played a double game. While they were talking to us about calming the situation down, simultaneously they were sending orders according to which Prozor had to be taken. Divjak raised that. The documents have already been admitted. So this is a very dirty, double game. On the one hand, they were talking to me and I was working as a dog, trying to calm the situation down; and, on the other hand, he writes that Prozor had to be taken from the direction of Here. Zejnil Delalic was also the same kind of player. He was saying one to me and doing another behind my back. We thought that he is just stupid, and he couldn't see things. We were wrong. The same thing was done by the BH Army in Rama. They had two plans. I received them, and they took it; Plan A against the Chetniks, and Plan B was against the HVO. And they had been preparing those two plans for months. And when people see that, it's very difficult to establish any sort of cooperation. After that, if you see somebody playing double games, games that are not played with an open heart, and I also had a very hard time, although I deliberately turned a blind eye to some things. Look at the documents. All these documents have already been admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: P00708, for example, is one of them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that this document also bears two stamps. We believed at the time Mr. Jaganjac, who had already become Mr. Izetbegovic's adviser for military issues, who also arrived in the area up there -- it's very difficult for me to give you the exact date. I recognise the dates in the documents. A joint stamp was crafted a bit later. On the 6th of November, I issued this order, and I believe that it was the basis of all my talks with regard to the joint command. And the elements were as follows: Firstly, that there should be order, order should be installed to roads. Not every fool should have been allowed to step out on the road, establish a check-point, and control whoever they wished. If there were check-points, the check-points had to be manned jointly by the HVO and the military police of the BiH Army. The composition at the check-points had to be determined based on the so-called ethnic parity or equal representation. Joint check-points had to be established within the next 48 hours. Ms. Nika, I can't see the rest of the document for the life of me. Can you help me out, Ms. Nika? While this is being done and while you're looking for a document that will help me out, I am going to see bullet point 5. This is something I drew everybody's attention to. A set of village guards in the villages, composed of people who were not in military units and issued necessary weapons to them. I knew well in advance -- well in advance that as the tensions mounted and when individuals and groups out of control, members of the HVO and BH Army who were not on positions, who were on furlough at home and had not handed over their weapons, it was impossible. I'm sure that this would be happening. It is a statistical given that I was sure that they would go to a village and commit a crime, and that crime would be described either to the BH Army or the HVO. And it was not a crime of the HVO or the BH Army, but a crime committed by an individual. In order to prevent this from happening, there should have been a joint command in place so as to provide for the establishment of village guards. In mixed villages, there were elderly people over the age of 60 who were to protect the villages from rift-raft, because none of the armies had at any level of administration or power to protect 50 or 60 villages in the municipalities of Rama from some rapist or a murderer who would creep into the village during the night. But that's why the necessary prerequisite was to arrive at a joint command. And then I also said that the weapons had to be handed over. There were plenty of weapons around. Everybody was armed to the tooth. Order had to be introduced to prevent anybody from turning up in any -- anywhere outside the front-line carrying arms. I believe that this document that I issued as a commander, although I repeat, you can see that I was tolerated both by the BiH Army and the HVO, they accepted me as such, I obviously -- in legal terms, I was not in a position to sign such a document. I did, however. I had drafted it. I adhered to it to this very day. And I go on to say that 64 members of the joint military police had to be provided to Prozor municipality, with a half/half composition, although there were more Croats there, but this is not how things should have been looked at. I managed to do some things, and some I failed. First we had some successes. Then it all crumbled, and then we would have to start all over again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The part that you couldn't read refers to the military police that were supposed to escort convoys and mixed joint patrols, but you've already spoken about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I would now kindly ask --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim once again that this was the basis or should have been the basis of the way of thinking on the part of the HVO and myself, as the forward representative of the HVO, and then this is how the relations between the HVO and the BiH Army should have been regulated. I did not meet with anybody's understanding. I would have installed order into the HVO, but Hanefija Prlic [as interpreted] and other such people in the BH Army -- I'm not saying that everybody in the BH Army was something like that. There were people in Bugojno for example with whom -- or partly in Travnik, there were people who wanted all this. There were people in the BH Army who sincerely wanted this, but there were also others who sincerely didn't want this, and there were a lot of them and their numbers grew by the day. And that's how the Mujahedin came, and as they kept on coming, the situation deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the record, General, could you please repeat the name of the person who could not be put under control? You said "Hanefija" --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Prijic, did you mean Prijic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Prijic, also known as Para. And some others in Vakuf were of the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now could you please look at document P00727 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the document we have before us has two stamps. The 6th of November, 1992, and there's a number also, 01-2496/92, this document is addressed to all HVO and ABiH members. When we read these documents and we look at the stamps, we may have the feeling that are a self-proclaimed commander of the joint command and you are giving orders to the HVO and the ABiH Army. These orders are detailed in items 1 to 11, and you impose a cease-fire in Prozor between 6.00 p.m. until 6.00 a.m. So far, you have told us, until this morning, that you went to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then you went back to Zagreb, and you were there to give a "helping hand," in inverted commas, to General Petkovic. This document does not fit in with this theory whereby you were providing support or aid. This is a document from a commander, a chief, somebody who is taking drastic measures and who orders a whole series of things. How can you reconcile your mission as a volunteer, coming to give a helping hand to your comrades, with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's just one explanation that is truthful, and this is as follows: In that job to create a joint command, I was accepted both by the Muslims and the Croats; hence, this was a job that already involved Mr. Jaganjac, working together with me. He had already been appointed an adviser to President Izetbegovic, and from his speech, I could conclude that at least verbally I was supported by Mr. Izetbegovic. Arif Pasalic had nothing against it. I believe that he stamped the document, but I'm not sure. Petkovic had nothing against this, because he was involved in the same job, he was trying, via Sarajevo, and I'm going to show today -- maybe today, if the book is prepared, when he went to Sarajevo to meet with Mr. Sefer Halilovic, who wouldn't meet with him, and said to his deputy, Croat, I don't want to talk to this Ustasha, they're all Ustasha down there. I'm going to show you this in a book. However, in legal terms, Your Honour Antonetti, you're absolutely right. There was no basis for me to sign this. This was the violation of the organisation of the army that you are familiar with. That's true, you are correct. However, given the state of chaos that reigned up there, I did, with the permission, meaning nobody objected, they gave me tacit support, I issued orders in the hope -- well, they did have a certain effect, they were successful, but my ultimate hope was that they would result in a joint command. In any other military, I would have been put into prison for having done a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely why I put the question to you. You give us a small detail. You said that Arif Pasalic put the stamp on here. Arif Pasalic, of course, is dead, and he will not be able to confirm this. Since you are under oath, do you ascertain that Arif Pasalic stamped the document as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think he did. After such a long time, I don't remember. I can't be sure that Mr. Pasalic -- the late Mr. Pasalic did it. What I'm saying is it seems to me that he was the one who did it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question of a technical nature: Why this document, which is an important one, and you mentioned what you wanted to do with it, why was this document not signed by Muslim, a Muslim, Arif Pasalic, Jaganjac, or some other person? Why didn't you think of having this signed by a Muslim authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from later documents you'll see that there are some signed by Mr. Jaganjac and by me and that there are other documents where I appoint a command for the return and liberation of Jajce, but all the documents are of the same type. Some are joint ones, with joint stamps. I don't know why this particular one wasn't signed by anybody. I can't remember the circumstances and the reason. But, anyway, they're identical documents, documents of this type that we're going to show later on referring to Central Bosnia, which, in view of my informal role, would be impossible in any other army. They wouldn't have had validity, and somebody would have locked me up if I were to write them of my own accord. But it is true and correct that Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac, and he was Izetbegovic's military adviser, and I, that we had - how shall I say this? - support, I from the HVO and he from certain BH Army structures, to try and do that. So you'll in the documents that I'm going to show you the extent to which this upset Sefer Halilovic and what he did until the end of April. He sent Jasmin Jaganjac packing, never to return to the army or politics, and that's when our final efforts fell through. And this went on for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have to have a break now. It is just about 12.30. We shall have a 20-minute break and return in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, please replace "cease-fire" by "curfew."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, turn to document P00720. If it's not legible, you can see it on your screen. That's your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave it some thought, and I'm almost certain that at the time when I signed this previous document, Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac had already taken the oath for the BH Army and that he had become -- he became the military adviser to President Izetbegovic. And we worked together, and we speak about an agreement to form a joint command, and that Juka Prazina's units should be placed under a joint command to be coordinated by Slobodan Praljak and Jasmin Jaganjac. So at that time he was quite certainly already the military adviser to President Izetbegovic, and in that respect I had the legitimate authority to sign orders of this kind because, quite simply, well, there was no opposition to that, especially since I had an ID from the BH Army. So, in a way, I was in both armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Would you now turn to document P00727, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This was also signed by you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we had to save Travnik after the fall of Jajce, because there was complete chaos, and after all the soldiers that were routed and stormed through Travnik and the enormous quantity of refugees, and the defence of Travnik, and then from the whole of Central Bosnia towards Sarajevo did not in actual fact exist. And I'll talk about that later on. But, anyway, I appoint a temporary commander, Blaskic. Ante Prkacin, who was a HOS general, that's how he represented himself, and he was confirmed as -- by Izetbegovic as a member of the BH Army. And then the third man was Mr. Arif Pasalic, who had arrived from Mostar and at that time was up there together with me. And this stamp on the left was made as a stamp of the joint command, and Jasmin Jaganjac issued instructions that this stamp be made up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at document P00776.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy chief of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the BH Army, Mr. Jovan Divjak here, in actual fact he confirms my order, and it says: "Signed by General Praljak" up there in the introduction. And he goes on to say that pursuant to that order, the HVO and the BH Army, he then issues a similar order for Jablanica, or Konjic and Jablanica. I don't know. Anyway, the essential point in this document is the fact that he conveys and confirms that my order was legal and lawful. And through the merits later on of General Petkovic and so on, we managed to move towards setting up a joint command, at least with some people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In the introduction to this document, it says that this was based on an agreement reached at an expanded meeting of the representative of the BH Army and representatives of the HVO Staff. Now, General, have you already spoken about that meeting to us here today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's difficult to remember all those meetings, there were so many of them. All I want to say is that I did not act as some idiot individual who came to meddle in affairs that didn't concern him. I went from Zagreb -- I left Zagreb because Franjo Tudjman certainly had agreements with Alija Izetbegovic, and then down there I managed once again, together with Jaganjac and Petkovic and Arif Pasalic and Prkacin, to try and do something, and I managed to defend Travnik successfully. And at that time, there were no conflicts. The conflicts were stopped. Some joint actions were decided and launched. We defended Travnik together, and until after the new year of 1993, that whole period, followed the right road, and gave us hope that we would be successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned Stjepan Siber's book. You wanted to refer to it. We haven't prepared for it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know that I'm always very much interested in the documents, and this is an important document which credits the other documents that we examined earlier. But to be absolutely certain, could you tell me exactly what the function of Jovan Divjak was within the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deputy chief of the Main Staff, the third-ranking person in the hierarchy or, rather, the second-ranking person in the hierarchy, because over there the chief was Sefer Halilovic, he was number one, and his deputy was Jovan Divjak. He was number two in the hierarchy of the BH Army at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now, the document comes in with the stamp from Jablanica on the date of November 20th -- to Jablanica, at the BH in Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right there. In the subsequent document, you will see that at that time Jovan Divjak came to the area. I believe that he was even arrested by some elements of the BiH Army, obviously those who -- Jovan Divjak is a Serb, he's a Serb. As far as I know, and there are documents to that effect, he was charged with something, and they kept him in custody, in prison. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did that. Some renegade commanders from Konjic arrested him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, below the title of the Staff of the Supreme Command, it says "IKM Konjic." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands for the forward command post. Every time when the Main Staff of the BiH Army sent a high representative to a place, the place where that person was sent was established as a forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And this order was sent to Jablanica, in the direction of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an order. He is ordering whatever he is ordering. I don't want to go on reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But the honourable Judge asked you whether he was in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was in Konjic. He was in Konjic, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As a representative?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at a forward command post there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, we have not prepared copies of Stjepan Siber's book for you. The general wants to refer to just one part of the book. The book will be prepared when we talk about Central Bosnia. However, if it's in well with the hitherto presentation of his --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the book's not in the e-court with a translation. The Prosecution objects to its being used at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Madam Pinter, there's a technical difficulty here, but you can get around that by asking the question about the book which was published by Mr. Siber and what was in that book regarding the topic we're discussing. You can deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will avoid that, but I'm going to give you the page number in e-court, which is 3D40-1167 in the English version. The document number is 3D03535. I've already said that, and the English page number is 3D40-1167.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, that's 3D0 -- I think what we have in the transcript has too many digits in it. Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One "0" too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's 03535? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, in Stjepan Siber's book, you wanted to point to a chapter that fits in nicely with what we have been discussing so far?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We will come back to the book, which is the war diary for the year 1992. The title of the book is "Deception, Misconceptions and Lies." I would like to refer you to a very short chapter that you said, and this is the 7th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: "Deception, Misconception and the Truth" is the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Siber, who was person number three in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he says that for that day a meeting was scheduled with a representative of the HV. In the morning, I was trying to convince Sefer Halilovic he had to persuade him, because I was informed that Petkovic would also be there, that he would also participate in the talks. Sefer turned this down, he refused to listen, and now he quotes: "Sefer, I don't want to talk to any Ustasha. "They're all Ustasha down there except for you." This is what Sefer says to Siber. Siber is a Croat, and that's why he's telling him that. He goes on. Siber answers Sefer, and I quote: "Sefer, what's your words? If you think that that statement of yours is something that I find appealing, then you are terribly wrong. "Very well. I was just joking," replied he with a cynical smirk. And then Siber kept on insisting attending the meeting which would also be attended by Ganic, Kljujic and others; and it would be pointless for him, Sefer, not to be there. And Sefer Halilovic replies: "Lie, Stjepan. Use any lie you want. Tell them I'm sick, that I have a high fever. Get me out of this mess." Vehbija Karic and Bena Fabijan [phoen] went to the meeting, and on behalf of the Herzegovina HVO, as they call it, which was not the Herzegovina HVO but just the HVO. We came to the building of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, Milivoj Petkovic, also Blaskic, Kostroman, Zarko Keza from VOS, who has already been mentioned here as the chief of VOS in the Main Staff of the HVO, and Bandic, the same Ivan Bandic who testified here not so long ago. And on the other side, there were Ganic, Kljujic, Dahic, Hebib, and a team from the BiH Army, minus Sefer Halilovic. He goes on to say that the meeting was joined by Generals Morillon and Razzak [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. President, I don't know that Ms. Pinter has found a way to get around the technical difficulty that the President identified a few moments ago. What is happening here is the general is reading a book, which, unless I'm wrong, somebody can maybe correct me, but I don't see any English translation anywhere, so he's just putting into the record, into the transcript passages of a book that we don't have translations for. It's unfair to do this to any party, including the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, from a technical point of view, you are right, but the fact is we do not have the book in the e-court system. General Praljak is under oath. You can imagine that he's not going to run the risk of reading anything different from what is on the page so that we then discover that there's been perjury. So when he is reading out of the book, he must be reading word for word. Now, as regards the translation, he's reading in his own language. The interpreter in the English booth has translated into English and in the French booth into French, so we're able to follow. Of course, if we do not have the book, with a full translation, we shall not be able to admit it as such. The question is whether or not this meeting took place. Apparently, yes, because Siber says that was the case. And when you interrupted General Praljak, I believe I heard that General Morillon was also present. You interrupted him at that point, so I'm not quite sure exactly what he intended to say at that point. This being said, there is a mistake in the transcript, but I don't remember which line it was. At a given point in time in the English text, it's stated "VONS," whereas I believe General Praljak referred to someone from the HOS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VOS, the Military Intelligence Service which was part of the Main Staff of the HVO. Zarko Keza was its representative. And in addition to General Morillon, there was also General Razzak Korvazak [phoen]. The book has been translated. I just -- since we are discussing this thing, I just wanted to show, and I did it on purpose, who was the one who was undermining all the efforts. When it comes to Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, his colleague from the JNA, General Petkovic, and all of us here, he sees all of us as Ustasha. And you will see later, in his other statements, for him we are Ustasha. Nothing could be established with this man. He was, and I can bring proof to that effect because the BH Army interviewed him, he was a KOS associate, the associate of the Counter Intelligence Service of the Yugoslav People's Army. This is what I'm trying to demonstrate, how the efforts fell through and why. Petkovic and his team, they all went to Sarajevo. Obviously, Morillon was aware of that. And then Sefer says, Lie, I'm not going, I'm not talking to Ustasha. He's going to repeat that in Geneva and everywhere else. This is the crux of what I am saying here. How come that painstaking efforts, which lasted for months, fell through, and why there was no cooperation between the Muslims and Croats, this sentence goes to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. You're saying that Halilovic played a game, so to speak, that wasn't along the same lines as Mr. Izetbegovic. That's what I've understood. But did he agree with the Young Muslims that we talked about yesterday, or was he dependent on the Serb KOS, K-o-s, or was he playing some other game?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A, he was not a Young Muslim, as far -- B, he was totally opposite to Izetbegovic and he undermined all of his efforts, and he says so in his book. And another BiH general, Muslimovic, also writes about that. He used the most derogatory terms when he talked about Izetbegovic. He called him an old fart. And this is the Muslim generals who talked about all that. He played his own game. Before the war, he was a member of KOS. Whether he remained that during the war, I leave it to others to be the judge of that. However, it is things like that that resulted in the attack of the BiH Army on the HVO, him and the like-minded people. For him, we were Ustasha. All Croats were Ustasha for him. And if he possibly signed something, he did it in bad faith, he did it only if he had to, under duress. Everything he did in the war until Neretva-93, 1993, everything was against the Croats, against the HVO; and this is what I am claiming, and this is what has been demonstrated. It's not that Praljak is confirming this. Siber is confirming this. General Muslimovic does it, too, in his own book. And Sefer Halilovic also confirms this in his book. And this is what I'm going to introduce, and I just wanted to show the honourable Judges why everything that I will go on exploring, why the whole efforts involving Jasmin Jaganjac and others fell through, not because the HVO wanted it to be so, but rather because these people from the BiH Army produced the conflict and attacked the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the information of the Chamber, the English translation is 3D02647. However, the page from which the general was reading is 3D40-1167. I misspoke, because we have two numbers for the back. One is for the Croatia version and the other is the English version, and that's why I made a mistake when I quoted the number of the first document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Pinter, when you quote numbers, please go a bit more slowly, because there are numerous mistakes. So please slow down when you read out numbers, because our interpreters do excellent work, but there are times when it's very difficult to follow at high speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best, really. Document number 3D02647, this is where you will find the English translation of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I appreciate counsel is giving me the reference, now that the general is finished reading from the book. It would have been useful five or ten minutes ago, but thanks anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I was not able to find it sooner.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could we now move to your testimony about Jajce, about the events preceding the fall of Jajce, during the fall of Jajce, and following the fall of Jajce, and your activities in that respect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, we have submitted a short file. The title is "Jajce 1992."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to recount briefly and refer to the global part. After the lull of Rama, Konjic, Vakuf and so on, I went back to Zagreb for a short time to deal with the affairs there, and then Dr. Gveric turned up, and of course I had heard the information, too, that Jajce was about to fall. Dr. Gveric asked for assistance with respect to the armoured bus, a monstrom [as interpreted] of a bus to pull out from Jajce, a monster.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And Dr. Gveric was where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Gveric from the HVO, from the Main Staff, the Health Service. Anyway, after we tanked up the bus and it set off, knowing what the situation was, I went, too, I went down there. The situation -- well, there was a repeated meeting with Petkovic, a hasty one, and then we tried to see if there was any chance of sending units which would help save Jajce. General Petkovic gave permission for some HVO units to advance towards Jajce. Secondly, some parts of the military police of the BH Army from Mostar were also supposed to -- or, rather, wanted to move towards Jajce. And, third, Prkacin, who was a HOS general and recognised by Izetbegovic as part of the BH Army, brought in a group of 400 people, 400 men, to Capljina, who somewhere from Croatia had reported as volunteers and said they wanted to go and defend Jajce. So this group of 400 men was more than 70 percent Muslim. In the Capljina barracks they were supposed to be equipped. And this matter with General Prkacin was done together with Bruno Stojic to provide clothes for them, to give them weapons if they needed some extra weapons and weren't equipped properly. And once they were equipped, they advanced on Jajce. And then -- and of course we have a precise report about all that. An unbelievable situation took place whereby the BH Army did not want to allow and, in fact, stopped these smaller units and this bigger one, because it was 400 strong. They would not allow them to pass towards Gornji Vakuf, and especially not from Gornji Vakuf onwards, where they held control. They didn't allow these units to advance and defend Jajce. That was, A, quite incomprehensible, and if there was any desire on their part to fight a joint battle, and, B, this was an indication that something was amiss, seriously amiss, in that whole play of theirs, and that they consider us anything else but their foes. And Prkacin, we'll come back to his report. We see how he -- what he tried to do. Anyway, these people were mistreated along that route for days, and they weren't able to break through at all and had to return ultimately. And the military police that was sent up there to help were unsuccessful; the HVO military police, that is. They weren't, nor was the BH Army police able to pass. They sent them back, too. So you can understand it from a different perspective altogether. Now, I, myself, managed to get through. I passed through all the check-points. Well, I know -- well, if somebody stopped me, I would shout at them, and while they would find their way, I would pass through. Anyway, the situation in Travnik was terrible. There was soldiers who had stormed through the town and left, and the HVO soldiers went to Herzegovina. Nobody could stop them. The BH Army soldiers went towards Vakuf. That's the brigade -- the Jajce Brigade that was set up in Jajce later on. But nobody stayed in Travnik. In Travnik, there was some BH Army command there, some sort of headquarters in a house that was called "Plave Vode," or "Blue Waters," and the command of Tihomir Blaskic, and the defence line simply did not exist. And when he managed to send his unit back because he wasn't able to get through, Prkacin did eventually get through. So Prkacin sent his men back, but he managed to get through. And then later on, quite a bit later on, Arif Pasalic arrived. At the beginning, I was alone with Blaskic, and then at my own initiative I took over the management of the chaos and the defence of Travnik. I tried to contain the chaos, because Blaskic was a trained soldier who commanded a battalion, and he had his remit. For example, after we toured the positions at which a line was to be set up to prevent the Serbs from breaking through, and the Serbs were advancing slowly - they would do a bit of shooting, then stay in the village and drink, so they didn't use military logic that a Western unit would take; otherwise, they would have passed through Sarajevo without any problems - and then this left the possibility open to us to establish something. Anyway, I asked Blaskic, and we'd established where we were going to do this, to take some work platoons and to dig trenches in the area, to put up a proper defence, and he knew how to do this. This was something that he knew how to do. But when he asked the people to come and help him out with planks of wood or whatever, some construction material, he would come back to me and say that nobody wanted to provide those materials and that they wanted to be given receipts for the issuance of those goods. I, of course, said, Well, fuck receipts. Write down whatever you want, man; threaten, force, do whatever you want. And at two exits to Travnik, I set up -- I put some people there who I saw were brave. I put some brave people there and said that nobody was going to leave Travnik unless they had a permit from me. The first person sent back from the check-point was the deputy of the number-one man in Travnik. He was a Croat. The number-one man was a Muslim. The number-two man was a Croat. So they asked him, Have you got a permit from Praljak? He said, No. They sent him back, and that was the group of people. And when he returned, there was a group of people standing around there to see what was going to happen. And when I asked the man, All right, where -- which direction did he go in, he said, I went to Split to start the defence preparations of Travnik. So here you have a political leader who is fleeing, and he has the gall to say that he was going to Split to begin preparations for the defence of Travnik, if you please. I kicked him in his ass, in front of all those people, to tell him, and to send a message to others of course, “I have positioned myself as the commander here and no fucking politician is going to fuck with me. I'm going to defend this town with these guys.” And we managed to dig the trenches, and let me tell you that shells were falling from the Serb side, Vlasic and elsewhere, on Travnik, and there was a hell of a noise. And knowing that the units -- well, there was some great guys on the Muslim side, Leho, a case in point from Turbe, but there were also those who couldn't care less one way or the other, whatever happened. And as I realised that the units that we would take out to take up these positions after the fall of Jajce would be very fragile and weak and would not be able to repel a Serb attack, I asked Blaskic go to the Bratstvo company, which was a manufacturer of military goods, to gather 100 men there the very next day. It was a matter of hours. You had to work quickly, to produce 100 guided mines, they are called "MRUD" in military terms, that can be placed 50, 60, 70 metres underneath the first -- the front-line positions, and electricity is used to activate them. They have a strong impact, and I was certain that when this explosive was laid down and that when the brave men, the men who were bravest, managed to ignite them and they exploded, that this would repel the Serbs and that this would give us a day or two to organise ourselves further. Now, it was 2.00 a.m., picture this, 2.00 a.m., no sleeping. I had just returned from a village beneath Mount Vlasic, where I went to see my men, and I found Blaskic talking over the phone obviously to the general manager of this company, and this went on for ages. It was a long conversation, and I asked him, Who are you talking to at such length, man? And he told me the name of the man from this company, Bratstvo. I took over the telephone receiver and told the managing director, because he had been given orders to go and produce this -- produce these explosives, and he asked me do I know what the time is, as if we were socialising and how come somebody dared wake him up at 2.00 a.m. Now, you have to know that the company was a major manufacturer of weapons in the former Yugoslavia and he was god there, so who are these Blaskics and Praljaks and whatever in -- to disturb him at that time of night, because he was a big boss. And after he said all this, after he uttered all this, and in Europe it is considered that the Hungarians have the worst swear words, as well as the Croats and the Italians, so I assume these swear words were made up of all those three nations, the swear words of all those three nations, the words that I uttered, and I said that I had sent the military police to arrest him, to take him to his company, to tie him to the radiator, and that at 8.00 in the morning I was going to execute him, shoot him. Now, Your Honours, of course I didn't execute him, and I had a cup of coffee with him a few days later, but at moments like that he had to take on responsibility. You had to take on responsibility and issue these orders and get results. Not only did I get these 100 MRUDs, these devices, but I got hundreds more later on. We set up our defence, to cut a long story short. The defence of Travnik was successful, and they did not manage to break through. And just one more detail. I don't know that we'll have time to look at it today. But, anyway, there was a unit made up of young men. They were up at positions. Two shells fell, I assume, and they fled. So that's just briefly, because you'll be able to see that on the footage. They're the films that I took later on as documentaries. I lined them up, I asked them why they were fleeing. I threatened them. I asked them who their officers were. A few men stepped forward and said that they were the commanding officers. And I said, Well, you go straight to prison, then. And the others said, Well, we'll go to prison, too, because they didn't want to go back, they wanted to go to prison. Now, faced with a situation of this kind, I thought, well, I'll send them to prison, but they can take off their uniforms, because they were uniforms of the Croatian people.
