So once again I had to threaten them. I said, Strip. And once they took their clothes -- their uniform off - it was cold - then they started backtracking, said they didn't want to go to prison, that they were ready to go back. Now, you have to turn the whole thing 'round. You did a bit of threatening. Then you had to become a paternal figure. And then I said to them, You're brave young men. You're going to do it. So these aren't military skills. They're only partially military skills. In this general disarray, and I'm telling you the facts and the events as they took place. And that completes my brief portrait of this picture. I managed to move the HVO and part of the BH Army to get them going, although certain parts, Refik Lendo, for example, who said that there were three reserve battalions, I wasn't able to get that at all. They hid them. Anyway, at meetings that we had, I was very precise and said that obviously they were keeping those battalions for settling of accounts with us because they didn't want to deploy them in the battle against the Serbs. The result was that Travnik was defended successfully, that Central Bosnia, that had no defence up to Sarajevo, was defended, and the way in which this is done I have described to you fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we have time. The film has been prepared. If you wish, maybe we can watch it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 3D03114, transcript number 2. This was submitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. There's a question before that, Ms. Pinter. Well, Witness, Mr. Praljak, once again I'd like to get back to my previous concern. The end result, well, was good. Order was established in Travnik. You obtained the weapons you wished to do have, but what I'm worried about is the method you used because you arrested the big boss, you tied him to the radiator, and you threatened to execute him. Of course, you didn't execute him, because on the following morning, or a few days later, you had a cup of coffee with him. But the question I have is this: Is this not something that is like a threat in the minds of your men? Were your soldiers also entitle to threaten people, to threaten to execute them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no. First of all, my soldiers, or the ones that remained, saw that there was somebody -- first of all, I received almost 1.000 MRUDs without which we would not have been able to carry out intention through. Second of all, the threat was just acting. Third of all, I appeared in public with that same man only two days later, and everybody knew that -- the most important thing. It is true that under normal circumstances I could be charged with threatening somebody, but this was a war, and somebody refused to obey an order after mobilisation. Your Honour, he was well due for execution. In any normal military, he would have been executed. The state was in a war. That company was not his private company. It was the property of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The general mobilisation had been called. The state of war was proclaimed. I could have easily executed him for having refused to participate in the defence of the state. Of course, this has nothing -- in a normal military, for example, in the Second World War in France or somewhere else, that same person would have been executed, court-martialed. My soldiers knew me too well, and really nobody in their right mind could think that I could really threaten somebody. So my joint appearance with him, the coffee, and another director from Vitez and so on and so forth, I stand by my behaviour. This was the matter of seconds. If I had given in to this man and if I had engaged in a discussion, like Blaskic did, Travnik would not have been defended. They would have marched on all the way to Sarajevo. I would have repeated all of my decisions, I've already told you, because my decisions are the expression of my way of thinking. Of what you are asking, a war is a war, decisions have to be made, I stand by my decisions, because between a threat to an idiot, who is a traitor of his country, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, 100.000 people in Central Bosnia or, in other words, Bosnia would have been divided in half, I did not think twice. This was the expression of my morale, of my military morale, of my idea of how to defend the country, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I listened to the question and I listened to the answer, and I'm not sure the answer was quite consistent with the question itself, because as I understand, the question was whether, through your actions, it would have given the wrong impressions to the soldiers, in other words, the green light for them to behave in a like manner. I believe that was the essence of the question. That needs to be answered, which wasn't answered, as opposed to what you indicated, which was for your own behave. So for that -- could we concretely answer, it could be beneficial to you and to others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General. The question put to you by my colleague was a question which aimed at the following: If a commander sets the example and flies off the handle, this can have an impact on his men. And as regards this particular aspect of the question, you did not answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] True. The example said by a commander is the most important thing in a war. However, you have to look at all of the examples said by that commander, and my soldiers were aware of all the examples of my behaviour in Capljina, in Mostar, in the defence of Travnik, and so on and so forth. They knew only too well how their commander was acting and behaving. An isolated example could have been wrong. However, the soldiers talk among themselves. All the HVO commanders and a majority of the soldiers of the BiH Army knew what my behaviour was from Capljina, on to Mostar, and then to Konjic and elsewhere, and they were talking about that. And my overall behaviour and my example was the way it was, the way you saw it. I would have given my own life to prevent somebody from committing a crime before my eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall adjourn for today, since there are only a few seconds left. But before doing that, I wanted to ask Mr. Kovacic this: A few weeks ago, I asked you to provide me with the list of documents which, according to you, are fake or forged. Since I am getting prepared for those questions I want to put to Mr. Praljak, I would have found it useful to have these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course we are aware of that, and we are working on that. Unfortunately, the problem was we were not able, for quite a long time, to identify all the documents mentioned in Mr. Praljak's testimony in the Naletilic case. There seems to be some confusion with numbers. We definitely know there was one which was in our case, but we have some problems in identifying some numbers in Naletilic which are those numbers in this case. We need like maybe -- I hope that in three days at most, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have already overstepped our time. As you know, we shall meet again tomorrow at 9.00. For Mr. Praljak's Defence, I would like you to know that you have already had 23 hours and 40 minutes. Thank you. And we shall reconvene tomorrow.
